title: Expose raw finish reason and AI Gateway log correlation on turn observations

labels.name: fix pending
labels.description: Fixed on a development branch; lands with the next release

body:
## Problem

A Workers AI model recently emitted native-looking tool-call syntax as assistant text instead of an OpenAI-compatible `delta.tool_calls` sequence:

```text
submit_customer_reply_draft:0{"draftAttemptId":"...","result":{...}}
```

Flue correctly preserved that as text and did **not** infer or execute a tool call. The provider defect is tracked separately with Workers AI. The difficult part was proving which boundary owned the failure from Flue observations alone.

The `cloudflare-ai-binding` provider sees the raw SSE `finish_reason` and the response headers, but the completed `turn` observation exposes only the normalized `response.finishReason` (`stop`, `length`, `toolUse`, etc.). It does not expose the original provider finish reason or an authoritative AI Gateway log correlation.

For Workers AI, `env.AI.aiGatewayLogId` is not a safe substitute: it reflects the most recent request on a shared binding instance and can be cross-attributed by concurrent runs. The response-level `cf-aig-log-id` header, when present, is tied to the actual response.

Without those fields, an observer cannot distinguish:

- provider `finish_reason: stop` with tool-call-shaped text;
- provider `finish_reason: tool_calls` whose structured fields were lost later;
- another provider-specific finish value normalized to the same Flue reason; or
- the exact AI Gateway request needed to inspect the raw stored response.

## Current path

The current released provider and current main have the same relevant shape.

`packages/runtime/src/cloudflare/workers-ai-provider.ts` currently:

1. reads `choice.finish_reason`;
2. maps it through `mapStopReason(...)`;
3. reads response headers for `options.onResponse`;
4. emits the normalized assistant message; and
5. later emits `ModelResponse.finishReason` from `response.stopReason`.

`ModelResponse` already carries `responseId`, `responseModel`, normalized `finishReason`, output, usage, and error.

## Requested change

Add allowlisted provider-response diagnostics to `ModelResponse` / completed `turn` observations, for example:

```ts
interface ModelResponse {
  // existing fields...
  providerFinishReason?: string;
  gatewayLogId?: string;
}
```

Exact naming is flexible. A generic provider request ID would also work if its semantics are documented. For the Cloudflare binding provider:

- retain the exact non-empty `choice.finish_reason` before normalization;
- read `cf-aig-log-id` from the response headers when present; and
- project both values onto the final `turn` observation.

Please keep the projection allowlisted. Do not expose arbitrary response headers, which may contain credentials or other unsuitable values.

## Non-goals

- Do not infer a tool call from assistant text.
- Do not execute `name:index{json}`-shaped output.
- Do not change the normalized `finishReason` contract.
- Do not make gateway correlation part of replay or execution identity. It is telemetry only.

## Acceptance criteria

- A Workers AI SSE response ending with `finish_reason: stop` emits both normalized `finishReason: stop` and raw `providerFinishReason: stop`.
- A response ending with `finish_reason: tool_calls` emits normalized `finishReason: toolUse` and raw `providerFinishReason: tool_calls`.
- `cf-aig-log-id`, when present on the response, is available on the matching completed turn observation.
- Concurrent binding requests cannot cross-attribute gateway IDs.
- Missing headers and finish reasons remain optional and do not break other providers.
- Tests cover header presence/absence and the `stop` / `tool_calls` mapping.

## Consumer mitigation

Our application is separately adding a bounded `useAgentFinish` continuation when its required terminal submit tool did not run. That protects the application invariant but does not replace provider-level diagnostics.

title: Preserve throw-site stacks in live error observations and OpenTelemetry exceptions

labels.name: fix pending
labels.description: Fixed on a development branch; lands with the next release

body:
### Describe the bug

Errors thrown by workflows and session operations lose their original stack before live observability can use it.

`serializeError()` reduces `Error` instances to `{ name, message }`, while `classifyError()` keeps only `{ type, name, code, message }`. As a result:

- terminal Sentry capture reconstructs a new `Error`, so the issue stack points at the telemetry bridge rather than the throw site;
- `@flue/opentelemetry` records an exception without `exception.stacktrace`.

This is visible in the Sentry example's `boom` workflow: the useful frame is where `boom.ts` throws, but that stack is gone before `observe()` receives the terminal event. The blueprint cannot recover it afterward.

### Expected behavior

Live observations and instrumentation should have access to the original throw-site stack. Durable run records and product events should not need to persist stacks by default.

A likely boundary is:

- add optional `stack` to observation-only `errorInfo` and attach it to failed run, operation, turn, tool, task, and compaction observations;
- keep durable `error` serialization as `{ name, message }`;
- have the Sentry bridge prefer `errorInfo` over the durable `error` value;
- have OpenTelemetry pass the stack to `recordException()` so it emits `exception.stacktrace`, subject to the existing content/redaction policy.

The main design question is whether stack traces should remain live-only or be persisted. Live-only seems safer because stacks can contain filesystem paths and other deployment details.

### Acceptance criteria

- A thrown workflow error observed in-process retains a frame from the original throw site.
- Persisted run events and run records remain stackless by default.
- OpenTelemetry exception events can include `exception.stacktrace` when allowed by policy.
- Default privacy behavior is covered by tests.

Related: #424, #460, #490, and discussion #181. #295 addressed capture-site stacks for `captureMessage`, not preservation of the original throw-site stack.

title: Preserve FlueError type and metadata in observation errorInfo

labels.name: fix pending
labels.description: Fixed on a development branch; lands with the next release

body:
### Describe the Bug

`ToolInputValidationError` carries a stable `type` (`tool_input_validation`) and structured `meta` containing the tool name and Standard Schema issues. When a tool error is emitted through `observe(...)`, `Session.classifyError()` projects the error to `{ type, name?, code?, message? }`, where `type` describes the JavaScript value (for example `Error`) rather than preserving `FlueError.type`, and `meta` is omitted.

As a result, observability consumers cannot distinguish validation categories structurally. They must parse the rendered message, including the `Arguments for tool ... do not match the required schema:` wrapper. This is brittle and makes it difficult to distinguish an application-authored validation issue from similar text quoted inside model-provided arguments.

This was observed with `@flue/runtime@0.4.0-nightly.202605130202`; the current `classifyError()` projection on `main` appears to have the same limitation.

### Expected Behavior

Observation error details should preserve the stable classification and structured metadata of known `FlueError` instances. For example, a tool input validation failure should expose `tool_input_validation` and its structured issues without requiring consumers to parse `message`.

An additive shape such as a dedicated `flueType` and sanitized `meta` would avoid changing the existing JavaScript-value `type` semantics. Only framework-owned `FlueError` fields should be projected; arbitrary enumerable properties from unknown errors should not be copied.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Define a tool with an input schema containing a custom validation issue.
2. Trigger a model tool call that fails that validation.
3. Register `observe(...)` and inspect the resulting error tool event details.
4. Note that `errorInfo.message` contains the formatted validation wrapper, while `ToolInputValidationError.type` and `ToolInputValidationError.meta.issues` are unavailable to the observer.

labels.name: fix pending
labels.description: Fixed on a development branch; lands with the next release

body:
### Describe the Bug

The Twilio channel turns a valid webhook handler response into a 500 response when that response comes from another Fetch implementation. The serializer checks the result with instanceof against the global Response constructor, so an otherwise valid cross-realm Response falls through to the invalid-result branch.

### Expected Behavior

A webhook handler response should retain its status and body regardless of which standards-compliant Fetch implementation created it.

### Steps to Reproduce

2. Make the webhook callback return a 202 Response created by node-fetch rather than the global Fetch implementation.
3. The channel returns 500 instead of preserving the 202 response.

packages/twilio/src/webhook.ts performs the instanceof check around line 335. Other channel serializers already use the cross-realm-safe Response brand check based on Object.prototype.toString, including the Zendesk implementation.

### Describe the Bug

The CLI blueprint parser accepts only LF frontmatter delimiters. On a Windows checkout with core.autocrlf enabled, tracked blueprint files are converted to CRLF and the CLI build fails before bundling.

### Expected Behavior

Blueprint frontmatter parsing should accept LF and CRLF line endings, so the build is independent of a developer's checkout conversion setting.

title: Node agents with the same instance id share queues and abort scope

labels.name: fix pending
labels.description: Fixed on a development branch; lands with the next release

body:
### Describe the Bug

Node durable submissions use a session key derived from the instance id but not the agent name. Two agents with the same instance id therefore share queue ordering, and aborting one agent instance also aborts the other agent's queued or running work.

### Expected Behavior

An agent instance is addressed by agent name and instance id. Work for alpha/shared and beta/shared must have independent queues and abort scopes.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Register two Node agents named alpha and beta.
2. Dispatch a long-running submission to alpha with instance id shared.
3. Dispatch work to beta with the same instance id.
4. The beta work remains queued behind alpha. Aborting alpha/shared also marks beta/shared for abort.

Admission constructs the key from only input.id in packages/runtime/src/adapter-helpers.ts around lines 170 through 174. The scheduler orders rows by that key in packages/runtime/src/sql-agent-execution-store.ts around lines 188 through 205. Node abort accepts an agent name but discards it in packages/runtime/src/node/agent-coordinator.ts around lines 597 through 616.

The session key and the corresponding ownership fences need to include both agent name and instance id across the storage adapters. Because this key is persisted, a fix also needs a coherent reset or migration strategy rather than mixing legacy and agent-scoped rows.

title: flue dev grants credentialed CORS access to arbitrary origins

labels.name: fix pending
labels.description: Fixed on a development branch; lands with the next release

body:
### Describe the Bug

flue dev reflects every Origin and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials to true. A site at an arbitrary origin can therefore make and read credentialed browser requests to the local development agent API when the application uses ambient credentials such as a SameSite=None cookie or cached HTTP Basic authentication.

### Expected Behavior

The development listener must not grant credentialed CORS access to arbitrary origins. It should either use non-credentialed CORS by default or require an explicit allowlist for local SPA origins.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Add route middleware that authenticates an agent route through a browser-sent credential.
2. Start the Node development server.
3. From an unrelated HTTPS origin, send a credentialed request or preflight to the local agent route.
4. The response reflects that unrelated Origin, permits credentials, and exposes the protected response to the caller.

The listener performs the reflection in packages/cli/src/lib/node-http-listener.ts around lines 31 through 60 and 163 through 170. flue dev enables this behavior unconditionally in packages/cli/src/lib/dev.ts around lines 338 through 347.

title: CLI build can erase a project through Windows output aliases

labels.name: fix pending
labels.description: Fixed on a development branch; lands with the next release

body:
### Describe the Bug

The CLI accepts an output directory that resolves to the project root through a Windows path alias. A differently cased drive letter or a directory junction to the root passes the textual output-versus-root check. The Node build then passes that directory to Vite with emptyOutDir enabled, which deletes the project before generating the build.

### Expected Behavior

The CLI rejects every output path that identifies the project root or source root, including existing symlink and junction aliases.

### Steps to Reproduce

2. Configure the Node target with output set either to the same root under a lower-cased drive letter or to a directory junction that targets the root.

title: Node target: crash-recovery latency is a hard-coded 30s lease + 15s scan; expose the knobs or fast-path takeover on boot
body:
## Summary

On the Node target (`flue dev` / `createNodeAgentCoordinator`), an agent submission interrupted by hard process death (SIGKILL, OOM kill, instance replacement) is not resumed for **~30-45 seconds** after the replacement process is healthy, and none of the timing is configurable.

## Mechanism (from `@flue/runtime` 1.0.0-beta.9 dist)

- A claimed submission holds a lease: `LEASE_DURATION_MS = 3e4` (conversation-stream-store), renewed by a heartbeat every `1e4` ms while the owner lives.
- After SIGKILL, heartbeats stop; the lease expires up to 30s later.
- The restarted coordinator's boot reconcile deliberately skips still-leased submissions (sound: it can't distinguish a dead owner from a live one), and the periodic lease scan (`LEASE_SCAN_INTERVAL_MS = 15e3`, `internal.mjs`) is what eventually re-drives the work.
- Worst case = lease remainder + scan interval. We consistently measure 32-37s from "server ready" to "[agent] … started" re-driving the interrupted submission.

## Measurements

Kill-mid-turn → restart → resume, same machine, live model, single-node:

| config | resume-to-settled |
|---|---|
| stock (30s lease / 10s heartbeat / 15s scan) | 32-37s |
| patched (5s lease / 2s heartbeat / 2s scan) | **12.1s** (dominated by the model turn itself) |

Patched = making the three constants env-overridable via `pnpm patch`; no behavior changes otherwise. The conservative design is correct for a multi-worker fleet, but on a single-node deployment the new process is provably the only possible owner, and 30-45s of user-facing downtime per deploy/crash is a lot to pay for a guarantee that isn't needed in that topology.

## Ask (either would help)

1. Expose `LEASE_DURATION_MS` / heartbeat / `LEASE_SCAN_INTERVAL_MS` as runtime config, or
2. A boot-time fast path for single-owner deployments: on startup, the coordinator takes over expired-or-orphaned leases immediately (or after one heartbeat interval) instead of waiting for the periodic scan — possibly gated behind an explicit `singleOwner: true` config.

Related but distinct: #457 (recovery blocked by stale activeAttempts) — this issue is about the *latency* of the healthy path, not a stuck one.

Happy to provide the harness we used (8-scenario durability suite driving kill/restart/resume against a live model) or test a patch.

title: Orphaned in-progress assistant messages left behind after interrupted submission attempts
body:
> _Originally reported by @lumpinif in [#478](https://github.com/withastro/flue/pull/478)._
>
> _All community-submitted pull requests are automatically converted to issues (bugs) & discussions (feature requests, enhancements) where they can be triaged and prioritized. Once prioritized, a PR implementation is created automatically._

### Describe the Bug

When an agent submission attempt is interrupted after `assistant_message_started` is persisted but before any content delta arrives, reconciliation classifies the attempt as `uncertain` and creates a replacement attempt **without** first terminalizing the orphaned in-progress assistant. If the replacement then settles the submission (e.g. due to a provider error), the orphaned in-progress bookkeeping from the original attempt survives permanently: every subsequent `user_message` append is rejected by the conversation reducer with `Cannot advance the conversation while an assistant message is in progress.`

The conversation is permanently unusable. The state is durable (persisted to SQLite in Cloudflare Durable Objects), so worker restarts do not help. No public API can repair it.

The root cause is twofold:
1. Reconciliation calls `recoverInterruptedStream` for `continuable` interrupted attempts but not for `uncertain` ones, even though `uncertain` attempts may have already persisted an `assistant_message_started` record.
2. The reducer's `submission_settled` handler does not clear in-progress bookkeeping for the settling submission, so orphaned attempt state can outlive the submission's terminal transition.

### Expected Behavior

When a submission settles (regardless of outcome), all in-progress assistant bookkeeping associated with that submission should be resolved. A settled submission should never leave the conversation in a state that blocks future appends. Specifically:

- Reconciliation should terminalize any orphaned `assistant_message_started` from a prior attempt before dispatching a replacement, even for `uncertain` attempts.
- `submission_settled` should act as a backstop that clears any remaining in-progress bookkeeping for that submission, since no writer can legitimately finish those messages after the submission is terminal.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Append the following records in order via the runtime's canonical writer: `conversation_created`, `user_message`, `assistant_message_started` (submission S, attempt A1), `assistant_message_started` (S, attempt A2), `assistant_message_completed` (S, A2, `stopReason: "error"`), `submission_settled` (S, `outcome: "failed"`).
2. Attempt to append a new `user_message` to the same conversation.
3. The reducer rejects it with `ConversationRecordInvariantError: Cannot advance the conversation while an assistant message is in progress.` — the in-progress state from attempt A1 was never cleared.

---

Original implementation from [#478](https://github.com/withastro/flue/pull/478) by @lumpinif

title: fix(runtime): clean up orphaned assistants after interrupted attempts
body:
Addresses #477.

- clean up an old started assistant before a replacement attempt runs
- clear leftover in-progress bookkeeping when a submission settles
- cover poisoned replay, active-tail preservation, and end-to-end SQLite reconciliation

Tested with:

- `corepack pnpm --filter @flue/runtime build`
- `corepack pnpm --filter @flue/runtime check:types`
- `corepack pnpm --filter @flue/runtime test` (48 files, 786 passed, 1 skipped)

This is a reference implementation for #477 — happy for you to close it and reimplement differently; the issue carries the full analysis.

title: Interrupted `uncertain` attempt leaves an orphaned in-progress assistant that permanently blocks the conversation

labels.name: fix pending
labels.description: Fixed on a development branch; lands with the next release

body:
### Describe the Bug

When a submission attempt is interrupted after `assistant_message_started` but before any delta, reconciliation classifies it `uncertain` and creates a replacement attempt **without** first terminalizing the old attempt's in-progress assistant. If the replacement then settles the submission (e.g. a provider error), the orphaned in-progress bookkeeping survives forever: every subsequent `user_message` append is rejected by the reducer with `Cannot advance the conversation while an assistant message is in progress.` The conversation is permanently unusable, the state is durable (DO SQLite), and no public API can repair it. We hit this in production on Cloudflare Durable Objects.

## Production trace (Cloudflare DO SQLite, beta.9)

Canonical stream of the poisoned conversation, reduced to the five relevant records:

| # | record | attempt | note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `user_message` | — | submission input applied |
| 2 | `assistant_message_started` | 1 | interrupted before any delta; **never completed** |
| 3 | `assistant_message_started` | 2 | replacement created by reconciliation |
| 4 | `assistant_message_completed` (`stopReason: "error"`) | 2 | provider error; closes attempt 2 only |
| 5 | `submission_settled` (`outcome: "failed"`) | 2 | submission terminal; attempt 1 still in progress |

From this point on, every new submission on this conversation fails at input-apply time with `ConversationRecordInvariantError`, before any model/tool work. Other conversations on the same worker keep working; worker restarts don't help (SQLite persists the stream).

## Root cause

1. The reducer intentionally tolerates concurrent in-progress assistants — `assistant_message_started` checks parent/tail and id uniqueness but not `inProgressMessages.size` (`conversation-reducer.ts` L316). That's what lets a replacement start before the old attempt is cleaned up. Fine per se — but it shifts the terminal-pairing responsibility entirely onto reconciliation.
2. Reconciliation honors that responsibility for `continuable` but not for `uncertain`: `agent-submissions.ts` L358–376 acquires the replacement attempt for both states, then calls `recoverInterruptedStream` only when `state === 'continuable'`.
3. The comment above that block says `uncertain` is safe to redispatch because *"nothing observable was persisted"*. That premise doesn't hold for the `input_only` resume mode: the `assistant_message_started` record **was** persisted, and it drives the reducer into an in-progress state that blocks the conversation's linear appends.
4. Settlement has no backstop: the reducer's `submission_settled` branch is a bare `break` (`conversation-reducer.ts` L552), so a submission can go terminal while its own attempt bookkeeping is still open.

## Why it cannot self-heal or be repaired after the fact

- Subsequent submissions never get their input applied (rejected at L791–792), so submission-level recovery never reaches the orphan — and it searches by the *new* submission's id anyway.
- Calling `recoverInterruptedStream` late doesn't work either: its `assistant_message_completed` append is rejected because the orphan's parent is no longer the conversation tail (L817) — the replacement moved it.
- The sessions surface has no inspect/repair primitive for this state, and deleting the whole session destroys legitimate history.

So the failure mode is: one unlucky interruption window (start persisted, no delta, then replacement settles) permanently bricks a durable conversation.

## Suggested fix — two invariants

**(1) Reconcile: extend the recovery call to `uncertain`.**

```ts
// agent-submissions.ts, reconcileInterruptedSubmission
if (state === 'continuable' || state === 'uncertain') {
  const replacement = await submissions.replaceSubmissionAttempt(...);
  if (!replacement?.attemptId) return undefined;
  if (state === 'continuable' || state === 'uncertain') {   // was: state === 'continuable'
    ... recoverInterruptedStream({ submissionId, attemptId })
  }
  return replacement;
}
```

Your own comment notes `recoverInterruptedStream` "self-guards to a no-op when there is none" — so widening the condition is safe: no orphan → no-op; orphan present → it appends the missing `assistant_message_completed(stopReason: "aborted")` exactly as it already does for `continuable`. The CAS-before-append ordering is unchanged.

**(2) Reducer: `submission_settled` resolves that submission's in-progress bookkeeping.**

```ts
// conversation-reducer.ts
case 'submission_settled':
  if (typeof record.submissionId === 'string') {
    for (const [messageId, message] of conversation.inProgressMessages) {
      if (message.submissionId === record.submissionId) {
        conversation.inProgressMessages.delete(messageId);
      }
    }
  }
  break;
```

Rationale: once a submission is terminal, attempt fencing guarantees no writer can legitimately finish those messages — the bookkeeping is provably dead. Deleting only the map entry touches neither `entries` nor `activeLeafId`, so committed history and the active path are unchanged. This gives three things at once:

- **Defense in depth**: any future path that forgets terminal pairing can't poison the conversation past settlement.
- **Retroactive healing of existing poisoned streams, with zero migration**: because every post-poisoning append was rejected (never persisted), a poisoned stream is a clean prefix — replaying it under the fixed reducer resolves the orphan at record 5 and the conversation just works again on next load.
- **Pure widening**: every stream the old reducer accepted reduces identically except for the dead bookkeeping.

We've been running exactly these two changes as a `pnpm patch` against the published beta.9 dist in production-like use, with a regression suite driving the real `SqliteConversationStreamStore` + real reducer over `node:sqlite` (poisoned-prefix replay heals; replacement history and tail preserved; next `user_message` appends fine; late writes from the replaced attempt are rejected by the ownership fence). Happy to share the full test file.

We're running exactly these two changes in production via a pnpm patch and I'm happy to send a PR — reference implementation follows below.

## Adjacent gaps in the same invariant family (for consideration)

1. **Non-direct submissions never emit a canonical settled record** — their settle path only updates the operational row (`failSubmission`/`completeSubmission`), so backstop (2) can't see them. If a dispatch-kind handler ever leaves an in-progress assistant, nothing resolves it. Suggestion: every submission kind's terminal transition should produce a canonically visible, reducible signal.
2. **The low-level stream-store `append` doesn't run reducer validation**, so a buggy/manual writer can persist a record the reducer will always reject — after which *every read* of the stream fails permanently (worse than the bug above). Might be worth a validating append at that boundary, or at least a loud doc warning that raw appends bypass the invariants.

### Steps to Reproduce

Append, in order, via the runtime's canonical writer: `conversation_created`, `user_message`, `assistant_message_started` (submission S, attempt A1), `assistant_message_started` (S, A2), `assistant_message_completed` (S, A2, `stopReason: "error"`), `submission_settled` (S, `outcome: "failed"`). Then attempt to append a new `user_message` → `ConversationRecordInvariantError: Cannot advance the conversation while an assistant message is in progress.` under beta.9 and current main.

title: No public durability binding site for dispatch-only agents (Cloudflare)

labels.name: fix pending
labels.description: Fixed on a development branch; lands with the next release

body:
## Context

On `0.4.0-nightly.202605121611`, durability is binding policy with three documented binding sites: `createAgentRouter(fn, { durability })`, a `start()` entry (Node), and `flue run` flags. We agree with the model — the runner decides, and the policy stays readable when a render crashes.

## Problem

A **dispatch-only agent on Cloudflare** — unmounted, reached exclusively through `init(...)`/`dispatch(...)`, which the docs explicitly support ("a dispatch-only agent stays unmounted and still works") — has *no* binding site. It silently runs on the defaults (`DURABILITY_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS` = 1 h, `DURABILITY_DEFAULT_MAX_ATTEMPTS` = 10).

That combination bites hardest in the documented orchestrator pattern (migration guide → Workflows → option 3): a Cloudflare Workflow step awaits `init(agent, { id }).dispatch(...)` under its own step timeout. When the outer step gives up (say at 20–25 minutes), an orphaned one-shot instance keeps retrying model work for up to an hour × 10 attempts with nobody waiting for the result — pure spend with no consumer.

## Workaround

`bindAgentDurability(identity, durability)` from `@flue/runtime/internal`, called at module scope in the agent module. It works (it's the same registry the public sites write through), but it's an internal import and it repeats the identity string.

## Ask

Any one of these would close the gap (in our preference order):

1. **Accept `durability` in `InitOptions` / the dispatch request** — the awaiting caller *is* the runner for a one-shot instance, so this is where the policy naturally lives; first binding wins for the instance.
2. **Promote `bindAgentDurability` to a public export** and document it as the binding site for dispatch-only agents.
3. A registration-level option in the generated Cloudflare entry (per-identity config), though that reintroduces config away from the runner.

Happy to send a PR for (1) or (2).

title: Export WORKERS_AI_OVERFLOW_MARKER / isAssistantContextOverflow / CloudflareAIBindingError from a public entrypoint

labels.name: fix pending
labels.description: Fixed on a development branch; lands with the next release

body:
## Context

The #428/#429 fixes (in `0.4.0-nightly.202605121611`) added exactly the right structure: `CloudflareAIBindingError` preserves status + bounded provider body, stamps the `WORKERS_AI_OVERFLOW_MARKER` on 413s plus `meta.reason: 'request_too_large'`, and `isAssistantContextOverflow` fronts both classification sites. Verified end-to-end against the installed nightly — 413 and context-length 400 classify, 5xx/429 don't, and a 413 with a rate-limit-shaped body now classifies correctly. Thank you — our boundary compensation and runtime patch are fully retired.

## Problem

None of the three symbols is exported from a public entrypoint (`.`, `./internal`, `./cloudflare`, `./cloudflare/internal`):

- `WORKERS_AI_OVERFLOW_MARKER` and `CloudflareAIBindingError` live in the hashed `dist/errors-*.mjs` chunk;
- `isAssistantContextOverflow` lives in the hashed `dist/registration-*.mjs` chunk.

Two consumer needs hit this:

1. **Regression tripwires.** Anyone bitten by the original overflow-classification gap wants a test asserting the chain (`new CloudflareAIBindingError({ status: 413, ... }).message` → `isAssistantContextOverflow(...) === true`) against the *installed* runtime, so a future repin can't silently break compaction recovery again. Today that test must glob hashed dist chunks and probe module exports by `fn.name` — it works, but it's coupled to bundler layout instead of API.
2. **Telemetry classifiers.** Applications that title/fingerprint provider failures want to strip or match the marker via the shared constant rather than a copied `"(request_too_large)"` string literal that can drift.

## Ask

Export from a public entrypoint (additive, no behavior change):

- `WORKERS_AI_OVERFLOW_MARKER` and `CloudflareAIBindingError` — `@flue/runtime/cloudflare` seems natural since the binding boundary is Cloudflare-specific;
- `isAssistantContextOverflow` — wherever fits (`./internal` would already be enough for test use).

Happy to send a PR if the entrypoint choice is agreed.

title: Expose platform environment bindings to deterministic Action handlers
@flue/opentelemetry drops tool error messages: empty exception.message and no span status message

labels.name: fix pending
labels.description: Fixed on a development branch; lands with the next release

body:
### Describe the Bug

When a tool errors, `@flue/opentelemetry` (1.0.0-beta.3, with `@flue/runtime`
1.0.0-beta.9) produces an ERROR span that carries no error text anywhere:

1. **`exception.message` is empty.** The runtime's tool-end observation
   (`type: 'tool'`) includes `errorInfo: FlueErrorInfo`, whose `message` field
   contains the real error text (populated by `classifyError` from the thrown
   `Error`). The tool-end handler ignores it: it builds the exception via
   `errorMessage(event.result)`, and on error `event.result` is the
   model-facing content array (`[{type: 'text', text: ...}]`), which
   `errorMessage` (string / `.message` object only) cannot unwrap. So
   `recordException` fires with an empty message while the message sits unused
   in `event.errorInfo.message`.

2. **The span status has no message.** `complete()` calls
   `span.setStatus({ code: SpanStatusCode.ERROR })` without a `message`.
   Trace UIs that render `status.message` (e.g. Arize Phoenix's spans-table
   "error" column) show nothing for error spans.

### Expected Behavior

For an errored tool span, the exception event's `exception.message` should
contain `errorInfo.message`, and ideally the same text should be passed as
the `message` in `setStatus`, e.g. in the tool-end handler prefer
`event.errorInfo?.message` over deriving from `event.result`.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a basic flue app with the OpenTelemetry instrumentation registered
   (`instrument(createOpenTelemetryInstrumentation({ content: { enabled: true, inline: true } }))`)
   and an `InMemorySpanExporter` on the tracer provider.
2. Register a tool whose `execute` throws:
   `throw new Error('bridge timed out after 20s')`.
3. Run a conversation turn that calls the tool, then inspect the finished
   `execute_tool` span: `span.status` is `{ code: ERROR }` with no message,
   and the recorded `exception` event has an empty `exception.message` —
   the text "bridge timed out after 20s" appears nowhere on the span, even
   though the tool-end observation's `errorInfo.message` contains it.

title: Cloudflare code-update reset leaves awaited agent dispatch pending until outer Workflow attempt fails

labels.name: fix pending
labels.description: Fixed on a development branch; lands with the next release

body:
### Summary

An awaited `init(agent, { id, uid: null }).dispatch(...)` running inside a Cloudflare Workflow step did not promptly settle after the target agent Durable Object was reset by a deployment. The agent trace recorded `Durable Object reset because its code was updated`, but the caller remained pending until Cloudflare Workflows failed the step with `WorkflowInternalError` after about five minutes.

The Workflow retry then found the create-only agent instance already present and had to treat it as an existing in-flight conversation. There was no prompt terminal result from the original awaited dispatch.

### Reproduction shape

1. From a Cloudflare Workflow step, await a dispatch to a create-only one-shot agent instance.
2. Let the agent begin a model turn.
3. Deploy updated agent code while the turn is active.
4. Observe the agent operation report a code-update Durable Object reset.
5. Observe the awaiting Workflow step remain pending, then fail with `WorkflowInternalError` several minutes later instead of receiving a prompt structured rejection or resumed result.

### Expected behavior

After a deployment reset, Flue should either recover the durable submission or settle the awaited dispatch promptly with a structured interruption error. The caller should not remain pending until an outer Cloudflare Workflow platform failure.

### Questions / suggested checks

- Is this another manifestation of the stale process-local attempt/controller recovery race described in #457?
- Can code-update recovery ensure the original `dispatch()` promise observes the replacement attempt or terminal settlement?
- Can the runtime expose a distinct code-update interruption/recovery outcome so an outer durable orchestrator can retry deterministically?
- A regression test where a Cloudflare agent fiber is interrupted by a code update while `dispatch()` is awaited from a Workflow would cover this boundary.

### Environment

- `@flue/runtime@0.4.0-nightly.202605101957`
- Cloudflare Workers Durable Objects
- Cloudflare Workflows caller
- Workers AI model call active at deployment time

The application also had ephemeral cross-turn state that needed to move to `usePersistentState`; that is being fixed application-side. This issue is specifically about the awaited dispatch remaining pending after the code-update reset.

title: Cloudflare interrupted submission recovery can be blocked by stale activeAttempts entry

labels.name: fix pending
labels.description: Fixed on a development branch; lands with the next release

body:
### Describe the Bug

With `@flue/runtime@1.0.0-beta.9` on Cloudflare, a durable agent submission can remain `running` indefinitely after its `flue:submission-attempt` fiber is interrupted. `onFiberRecovered()` correctly calls `requestSubmissionRecovery()`, but `reconcileSubmissions()` skips the submission while its attempt key remains in the process-local `activeAttempts` set:

```js
if (this.activeAttempts.has(this.submissionAttemptLocalKey(submission))) continue;
```

The attempt-marker guard immediately below it already lets `recoveryRequestedAt` override a marker, but the local-active guard does not. If the interrupted `runFiber()` promise does not settle, its `.finally()` never clears `activeAttempts`; each 30-second `__flueWakeAgentSubmissions` callback then skips the submission again.

We observed one submission recover only after the stale local attempt eventually cleared, while another remained in this wake loop for the full capture. Sanitized diagnostics for the stuck case were one `fiber:run:interrupted` after about 29 seconds, one `fiber:recovery:handled` with `status: "user"`, then only `schedule:execute` / `schedule:create` every 30 seconds, with no replacement `fiber:run:started` or terminal `submission_settled`.

There is a related controller race: attempts share `activeControllers[submissionId]`. If recovery starts replacement attempt B while old attempt A’s promise remains unsettled, A’s delayed `.finally()` unconditionally deletes that map entry and can remove B’s controller. Cleanup should only delete when the stored value is A’s captured controller.

### Expected Behavior

A durable recovery request should override stale process-local activity state and immediately reconcile the interrupted attempt. A late cleanup from the old attempt should not remove the replacement attempt’s controller.

A minimal fix appears to be:

```js
if (
  this.activeAttempts.has(this.submissionAttemptLocalKey(submission)) &&
  submission.recoveryRequestedAt === void 0
) continue;
```

and identity-guarding controller cleanup:

```js
if (this.activeControllers.get(submission.submissionId) === controller) {
  this.activeControllers.delete(submission.submissionId);
}
```

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Start a Cloudflare durable agent submission and keep its `runFiber()` promise pending long enough for the Workers invocation/fiber to be interrupted.
2. Let Agents SDK recovery invoke `onFiberRecovered()` with the stashed `submissionId` and `attemptId`.
3. Keep the old promise unsettled so its `.finally()` does not remove the process-local attempt key.
4. Observe that `requestSubmissionRecovery()` persists the request, but immediate reconciliation and subsequent 30-second wake callbacks skip the running submission and never start a replacement fiber.

Environment: `@flue/runtime@1.0.0-beta.9`, Cloudflare Workers, `agents@0.17.x`.

title: Feature request: dynamic tool discovery/loading (like Mastra's ToolSearchProcessor) to avoid putting hundreds of tools in the agent context
body:
## Problem

When an agent has access to a large tool library (hundreds of tools), putting all tool definitions into the model context upfront is expensive in tokens and can degrade tool-selection quality. I'd like a built-in way to keep tools out of the context by default and let the agent discover/load them on demand.

## Proposed solution

Something similar to Mastra's `ToolSearchProcessor`: https://mastra.ai/reference/processors/tool-search-processor

The idea: instead of exposing every tool upfront, expose two meta-tools to the agent:

- `search_tools` — the agent searches the tool library by keywords and gets back the top matches.
- `load_tool` — the agent activates a specific tool so it becomes available on the next turn.

Nice-to-have options seen in the Mastra design:

- `topK` / `minScore` to control search results.
- An `autoLoad` mode that activates matched tools directly from the search step, collapsing the two-step (search → load) flow into one.
- Loaded-tool state tracked either in-memory (per thread, with TTL) or derived from conversation messages so it's restart-safe.
- A request-aware `filter` hook to hide/block certain tools per request.
- Cache-friendly behavior (append-only loads so the cached prompt prefix stays stable).

## Why

This would let Flue agents scale to large tool sets without paying the upfront context cost for every tool, keeping only the meta-tools plus whatever the agent actually needs loaded.

## References

- Mastra ToolSearchProcessor reference: https://mastra.ai/reference/processors/tool-search-processor

title: defineTool run() receives no toolCallId, so a tool cannot correlate its execution with its own tool events

labels.name: fix pending
labels.description: Fixed on a development branch; lands with the next release

body:
## Summary

Every observable surface of a tool call carries a `toolCallId` — the `tool_start` and `tool` events, `LlmToolResultMessage`, observations — except the one handed to the tool implementation itself: the `ToolContext` passed to a `defineTool`'s `run()` is only `{ input, signal }`. A tool cannot correlate its own execution with the events it emits, or key application state on the specific call that invoked it.

## Evidence

`Session.createCustomTools` (`packages/runtime/src/session.ts`) wraps every `defineTool` via `this.wrapModelTool(tool, 'custom', (_toolCallId, params, signal) => …)` — the prepare callback receives the model turn's tool call id as its first parameter but binds it as `_toolCallId` and never forwards it, calling `parseToolInput(toolDef, params, signal)` (`packages/runtime/src/tool.ts`), which builds the run context as only `{ input, signal }`. The surrounding `wrapModelTool` stamps that same id on the `tool_start`/`tool` events it emits, so the id exists everywhere except inside `run()`.

## Why this matters

Tools that create durable, addressable side effects need to name them after the call that raised them — for example registering a pending approval/confirmation record that a later event-stream consumer resolves by matching the tool event's `toolCallId`. Without the id in `ToolContext`, the tool has to mint its own correlation key and the application has to maintain a mapping between that key and the real tool event ids, or give up on correlating entirely.

## Expected behavior

`ToolContext` carries a `readonly toolCallId: string` that matches the `toolCallId` on the tool's emitted events.

## Current workaround

A downstream application patches `@flue/runtime` (1.0.0-beta.9) to rename the discarded parameter and spread it into the run context — a two-line change at the wrap site plus the type field.

Implemented with tests on a fork branch (`parseToolInput` turns out to be the only place a `ToolContext` is constructed, so the field can be required; the internal no-model path synthesizes an id the same way action invocation ids are minted): https://github.com/steven4354/flue/commit/bb9d7753c2bfdaa22675bb94b1cb1f258d285ed1

title: A sandbox tools factory silently drops the framework default tool surface

labels.name: fix pending
labels.description: Fixed on a development branch; lands with the next release

body:
## Summary

When a `SandboxFactory` supplies a `tools` factory, the factory's return value replaces the framework default tool list (`read`, `write`, `edit`, `bash`, `grep`, `glob`) rather than composing with it, and there is no public way to rebuild that default set — the builder is internal to the runtime and not exported from `@flue/runtime`. An app that supplies a factory just to add one custom tool silently ships an agent with no file or shell tools.

## Root cause

Session initialization uses the sandbox factory's `tools` result as the complete tool list whenever the field is present; the defaults are installed only when it is absent. The default list is built by the internal `createTools()` in `packages/runtime/src/agent.ts`, which the package entry does not export, so a `tools` factory cannot reference it. Nothing fails at build or startup — the loss surfaces later as the model reporting it cannot read or edit files.

## Why this matters

Anyone wrapping an external sandbox who wants the stock tool surface plus their own additions hits this. The only options today are hand-reimplementing all six tools against `SessionEnv` or patching the package to re-export the internal builder.

## Expected behavior

A public export returns the same default tool list the framework installs when no `tools` field is present, so a factory can spread it and append its own tools.

## Current workaround and tested fix

A downstream application carries a pnpm patch on `@flue/runtime@1.0.0-beta.9` re-exporting the internal builder so its agent composes the defaults with multimodal adapter tools. A source-level fix is implemented with tests on a fork branch: a public `createDefaultTools(env, { subagents?, packagedSkills? })` wrapper (the internal `task` option stays internal, and the `task` tool is excluded because the framework appends it separately even when a factory is supplied). New tests cover the default names from the public entry and a factory composing the defaults plus a custom tool; the full runtime suite, typecheck, and build are green: https://github.com/steven4354/flue/commit/8a8746e90d0f0490b516db8ee857b83913795a66

title: dispatch() of a kind:'signal' message always starts a model turn, so context-only events cannot be delivered to an idle agent
body:
## Summary

Delivering a `kind: 'signal'` message through `dispatch()` (or the direct agent POST, which shares the same wire shape) always admits a durable submission that is processed to completion: the runtime appends the signal record and immediately runs a full model turn, producing an assistant response nobody asked for. There is no delivery mode, alternate API, or route that lands a signal while the agent is idle so the model consumes it only on the next externally-triggered turn.

## Evidence

Traced on current main (c5e7ef4):

- `AgentDispatchRequest` is `{ id, message }` and `DeliveredMessage` is `kind: 'user' | 'signal'` with no delivery flags (`packages/runtime/src/types.ts`), so a signal cannot be marked context-only at the wire.
- `enqueueDispatch` enqueues unconditionally (`packages/runtime/src/runtime/dispatch.ts`), and the queue's only consumers — the Node and Cloudflare coordinators' claim loops — both call the shared `processSubmission`.
- `processSubmission` never branches on `message.kind` (`packages/runtime/src/runtime/agent-submissions.ts`); a signal takes the same path as a user prompt into `session.processSubmissionInput`.
- In `packages/runtime/src/session.ts`, `runPersistedSubmissionInput` documents itself as "the single input path for both a direct HTTP prompt and a `dispatch()` call", and `runPersistedContextInput` appends the canonical record then unconditionally awaits `resumeConversationToCompletion`. A fresh input with no assistant after it classifies as `resume`/`input_only`, whose documented contract is "start the first turn" — a real provider call, since `toTurnMessage` renders the signal into model context as a user message.
- The `dispatch()` doc says "It does not wait for model processing" — fire-and-forget means not-awaited, not not-processed, so the per-signal model turn is easy to miss until the bill or the transcript shows it.

## Why this matters

The callers signals are documented for — channels modeling multi-user conversations, applications recording out-of-band events (a webhook, another participant's message, a human resolving a pending approval) — mostly want the event to inform the next turn, not provoke one. Today every ambient event costs its own LLM call and injects an unprompted assistant reaction into the durable transcript.

## Expected behavior

A signal delivery can opt out of waking the agent: the record persists durably and reaches live conversation observers, and the model consumes it whenever the next turn is started by something else. An explicit per-dispatch delivery mode would suffice.

## Current workaround

A downstream application patches `@flue/runtime` (1.0.0-beta.9) to expose an out-of-turn append that writes the canonical signal record through the agent coordinator's own conversation writer: live subscribers receive the UI chunk immediately, no turn runs, and the append throws while an assistant turn is in progress so the reducer's linear-append invariant holds.

title: observe(): no event carries partial tool-call arguments (pi-ai toolcall_delta is dropped)

labels.name: fix pending
labels.description: Fixed on a development branch; lands with the next release

body:
### Summary

The runtime's conversation stream store forwards pi-ai streaming events to
Flue events for assistant text and thinking, but silently drops
`toolcall_delta`. There is no Flue event type that carries partial tool-call
arguments, and `session.task()` has no per-call streaming callbacks, so an
application cannot observe a tool call's argument text while the model is
still emitting it — only the completed arguments at `toolcall_end`.

### Where the drop happens

In `conversation-stream-store` (`dist/conversation-stream-store-*.mjs`,
`case "message_update"`):

- `text_start` / `text_delta` / `text_end` → canonical `assistant_text_*`
  records + emitted `text_delta` events
- `thinking_start` / `thinking_delta` / `thinking_end` → canonical
  `assistant_reasoning_*` + emitted `thinking_*` events
- `toolcall_end` → canonical `assistant_tool_call` (complete arguments)
- **`toolcall_start` / `toolcall_delta` → no branch; dropped**

The deltas demonstrably exist upstream of the drop: the runtime's own
OpenAI-compat streaming adapter produces them
(`stream.push({ type: "toolcall_delta", contentIndex, delta, partial })` in
`dist/cloudflare/internal.mjs`).

### Use case

An application can submit its primary artifact as tool-call arguments to a
schema-enforced submit tool. That boundary is deliberate: moving the artifact
body into assistant text would double output-token cost and weaken the
schema-enforced submit contract. To stream a live preview while preserving
the submit-tool boundary, the application needs the partial argument text of
that tool call as it is generated: it can tap the argument stream in-process,
incrementally extract one JSON string field, and push coalesced deltas to its
own UI channel.

### Requested behavior

Forward `toolcall_delta` as a Flue observation event delivered to
`observe()` subscribers, carrying at least:

```ts
{
  type: "toolcall_delta",
  toolCallId: string,
  toolName: string,
  argumentTextDelta: string, // raw partial-JSON argument text chunk
}
```

Constraints that keep the change cheap:

- **In-process only.** Deliver to `observe()` subscribers like the existing
  `text_delta`/`thinking_*` events; explicitly exclude the event from
  buffered run streams and persisted stores. No storage or replay
  obligations — per-token persistence is exactly what we need to avoid.
- No change to `toolcall_end` / canonical `assistant_tool_call` semantics;
  complete arguments remain the source of truth.
- `toolcall_start` forwarding would be nice for symmetry (it carries the
  tool name before the first delta) but is not required if
  `toolcall_delta` includes `toolName`.

### Alternatives considered

- Streaming the artifact as assistant text before the submit tool call: pays
  for the body twice in output tokens and weakens the schema-enforced
  submit boundary.
- Polling materialized views faster: never exposes partial arguments at any
  poll rate; multiplies read load.
- Patching the runtime locally: feasible as a pinned patch, but this seems
  useful as a runtime capability.

title: Parallel tool execution has no concurrency limiter — 5+ codemode tool calls in one turn trip Cloudflare's 4-concurrent-dynamic-worker platform limit
body:
## Context

Same production setup as #439: a persistent per-case support agent deployed on Cloudflare, with the workspace `code` tool backed by `@cloudflare/codemode`'s `DynamicWorkerExecutor` through a Worker Loader binding (the cf-shell connector extracted from core in 0.8.0).

Cloudflare enforces a hard platform limit on Worker Loaders: **max 4 concurrent dynamic worker invocations per request** ("Limit for up to 4 concurrent dynamic worker invocations per request. It's a limit to protect the platform.").

## Problem

Flue hard-codes fully parallel tool execution with no concurrency knob:

- `src/conversation-stream-store` constructs the pi-agent-core `Agent` with `toolExecution: "parallel"` (dist `conversation-stream-store-*.mjs`, `new Agent({ ..., toolExecution: "parallel" })`) — not configurable from app code;
- pi-agent-core's `executeToolCallsParallel` runs every tool call in an assistant turn under an **unbounded `Promise.all`** (`agent-loop.js`);
- `@cloudflare/codemode@0.3.8` mints a **fresh dynamic worker per execution** (`this.#loader.get(`codemode-${crypto.randomUUID()}`, ...)`, `dist/index.js:232`) and `DynamicWorkerExecutorOptions` exposes no queue/concurrency option.

So the moment the model emits 5+ `code` tool calls in a single turn — which "batch your independent reads in one step" prompting actively encourages — the request trips the platform limit and the surplus calls fail:

```
Error: native tool failure: code (dynamic-worker-capacity)
reason: Too many concurrent dynamic workers
toolCallId: functions.code:6
```

The failure does flow back to the model as a tool error and it can self-correct, but it burns turns and degrades output quality on a hot path.

The only escape hatch today is declaring `executionMode: "sequential"` on the tool, but pi-agent-core downgrades the **entire batch** to sequential when any tool in the turn declares it — punishing the cheap fetch-based tools batched alongside a single `code` call.

## Ask

Expose a limiter so dynamic-worker-backed tools can be capped without serializing the whole turn. Any of these shapes would work:

1. **Per-tool bounded concurrency**: extend `executionMode` to accept `{ maxConcurrency: number }` (or a sibling `maxConcurrency` field), applied per tool name inside `executeToolCallsParallel` while the rest of the batch stays fully parallel;
2. **Agent-level knob**: let `toolExecution` accept `{ mode: "parallel", maxConcurrency }` and plumb it through the coordinator config;
3. **Built-in queueing in the codemode path**: a semaphore around `DynamicWorkerExecutor.execute` defaulting to ≤4 — since Flue targets Cloudflare first, tripping a documented platform limit under the framework's own default execution mode is arguably a framework defect, and a safe default here fixes every consumer.

Option 1 (per-tool cap honored by the loop) composes best with the existing `executionMode: "sequential"` semantics; option 3 is the smallest and could ship independently.

## Workaround

We own the extracted cf-shell connector, so we are wrapping `executor.execute` in a module-level semaphore capped below the platform limit. That fixes our copy only — every other Cloudflare consumer of the connector + codemode pairing hits the same wall under default settings. Happy to send a PR for whichever shape you prefer; would love this in `1.0.0-beta.10`.

Versions: `@flue/runtime` 1.0.0-beta.9 (pinned at c5e7ef45), `@cloudflare/codemode` 0.3.8.

title: thinkingLevel is silently dropped for models registered via registerProvider()

labels.name: fix pending
labels.description: Fixed on a development branch; lands with the next release

body:
### Describe the Bug

When an app forwards a `thinkingLevel` for a model registered via `registerProvider()` whose id is not in pi-ai's catalog (gateway presets, OpenRouter `@preset/...` ids), the level is silently dropped. The resolved model hydrates with `reasoning: false`, the registration API offers no way to override it, and pi-ai skips thinking emission for non-reasoning models — so the outgoing request carries no `reasoning` field and the model answers without thinking. No error is raised anywhere. Catalog models are unaffected; this hits exactly the gateway and preset ids that `registerProvider()` exists for. Sibling of [#418](https://github.com/withastro/flue/issues/418), which is the same missing override for `input`.

### Expected Behavior

A registration can declare a model as reasoning-capable, mirroring the existing `contextWindow`/`maxTokens` overrides at registration and per-model level, so that a forwarded `thinkingLevel` reaches the wire (e.g. OpenRouter's `reasoning: { effort }`).

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Register a provider with a reasoning-capable model id the catalog doesn't know (e.g. an OpenRouter `@preset/...` id)
2. Resolve the model and observe `reasoning` is `false`, with no registration option to change it
3. Prompt with `thinkingLevel: 'high'` and capture the outgoing request: it contains no `reasoning` field, and the model responds without thinking

Tested patch (registration-level + per-model `reasoning` override, mirroring the `contextWindow`/`maxTokens` layering; full runtime suite and `tsc --noEmit` green): https://github.com/steven4354/flue/commit/3bc9feda5c8e4fea7d31d63e63b76e9f1e1d173c

title: feat: add A2A protocol channel for agent-to-agent communication
body:
## Summary

Adds `@flue/a2a` — a channel adapter that makes any Flue agent speak the [A2A (Agent-to-Agent) protocol](https://a2a-protocol.org/) for inter-agent discovery and messaging.

## Why

The A2A protocol enables interoperability between AI agents across different frameworks. With this channel, Flue agents can be discovered and messaged by any A2A-compatible client — including agents built with ADK, LangChain, CrewAI, or other frameworks.

## What it does

- **Agent Card**: serves `/.well-known/agent-card.json` so other agents can discover this agent's capabilities
- **message/send**: accepts A2A JSON-RPC messages and routes them to the Flue agent
- **Task lifecycle**: tracks task state (submitted → working → completed/failed)
- **Skills**: maps Flue skills to A2A skill descriptors

## How to test

```bash
cd packages/a2a && npm install && npm start

# Discover
curl http://localhost:3000/.well-known/agent-card.json

# Send message
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/ \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"message/send","params":{"message":{"messageId":"1","role":"user","parts":[{"kind":"text","text":"Hello"}]}},"id":"1"}'
```

## Files

- `packages/a2a/src/index.ts` — Channel factory and HTTP server
- `packages/a2a/src/handlers.ts` — A2A JSON-RPC method handlers
- `packages/a2a/src/types.ts` — A2A protocol type definitions
- `packages/a2a/src/errors.ts` — A2A error codes
- `packages/a2a/README.md` — Usage docs

## A2A Protocol

The [A2A specification](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification/) is governed by the Linux Foundation with 150+ supporting organizations. This implementation targets protocol version 1.0.

title: Workers AI "Stream ended without finish_reason" thrown by provider but not classified retryable, so it hard-fails instead of retrying

labels.name: fix pending
labels.description: Fixed on a development branch; lands with the next release

body:
`@flue/runtime`'s Cloudflare Workers AI streaming provider throws `Stream ended without finish_reason` when a Workers AI SSE stream ends before any chunk carries a `finish_reason` (`packages/runtime/src/cloudflare/workers-ai-provider.ts:553`; surfaced as `stopReason: 'error'`, `errorMessage: 'Stream ended without finish_reason'` in the catch handler at `:582-583`). This is known, Cloudflare-acknowledged Workers AI behavior (their own `workers-ai-provider` adapter changelog added "premature stream termination detection"), and it shows up more often under concurrent load.

`isRetryableModelError()` (`packages/runtime/src/submission-state.ts:295-300`) is meant to route exactly these transient model failures into Flue's built-in in-loop retry (3 attempts, exponential backoff). Its regex —

```
overloaded|rate.?limit|too many requests|429|500|502|503|504|service.?unavailable|server.?error|network.?error|connection.?(?:reset|refused|lost)|socket hang up|fetch failed|timed? out|timeout|terminated
```

— has no branch matching `stream ended without finish_reason`, so the error is classified as permanent and the submission hard-fails immediately instead of retrying.

The result is an internal self-inconsistency in one package: the provider layer treats premature stream termination as a transient error, but the retry-classification layer treats that same error as permanent. Flue detects the problem correctly; it just doesn't retry it. (`durability.maxAttempts` doesn't help here either — it covers submissions found interrupted after a process/DO restart, not a synchronous in-flight throw.)

Confirmed present on current `main` (`v1.0.0-beta.9-22-gc5e7ef45`).

## Repro (deterministic, classifier-level)

```ts
isRetryableModelError({
  role: 'assistant',
  stopReason: 'error',
  errorMessage: 'Stream ended without finish_reason',
  content: [],
});
// expected: true
// actual:   false
```

## Proposed fix

- Minimal: add `stream ended without finish_reason` to the `isRetryableModelError` regex.
- Better long-term: tag this failure with a structured `retryable` flag (or reason code) at the throw site instead of relying on downstream free-text regex matching. The same fragility affects `mapStopReason`'s default branch, which produces `Provider finish_reason: ${reason}` (`packages/runtime/src/cloudflare/workers-ai-provider.ts:194-198`) — also free-text and unmatched by the classifier.

The existing test "surfaces a provider error when the stream ends without a finish_reason" (`packages/runtime/test/cloudflare-workers-ai-provider.test.ts:723`) should stay green — the fix belongs in classification, not in suppressing the surfaced error.

## Impact / workaround

In production this manifested as intermittent hard failures under concurrent Workers AI load, where the only recovery was an app-level timeout fallback minutes later. We're currently carrying a local `pnpm patch` that adds the string to the regex; we'd like to drop it once this is fixed upstream.

title: OperationFailedError loses structured operation and reason data
body:
> _Originally reported by @hiro-nikaitou in [#440](https://github.com/withastro/flue/pull/440)._
>
> _All community-submitted pull requests are automatically converted to issues (bugs) & discussions (feature requests, enhancements) where they can be triaged and prioritized. Once prioritized, a PR implementation is created automatically._

### Describe the Bug

`OperationFailedError` in `packages/runtime/src/errors.ts` hardcodes its `details` field to an empty string (`''`) and omits `meta` entirely. When a dispatched operation fails, the serialized error contains no structured data — the operation name and underlying failure reason are only embedded in the prose `message` string.

This means downstream error trackers must regex-parse the message to recover the operation name and reason. Because the message includes a unique dispatch UUID, every occurrence appears as a distinct error, breaking issue grouping and preventing programmatic classification.

### Expected Behavior

`OperationFailedError` should populate `details` with the failure `reason` and include `{ operation, reason }` in `meta`, matching the pattern used by other `FlueError` subclasses (e.g. `CloudflareAIBindingError`, `AttachmentLoadingError`). This allows consumers to inspect structured fields via `instanceof` checks and structured data rather than parsing message text.

### Steps to Reproduce

<!-- Either starting from one of the examples in `examples/`, or from a basic hello world. -->

1. Trigger a dispatched operation that fails (e.g., dispatch an agent input that results in an error).
2. Catch the resulting `OperationFailedError`.
3. Inspect the error's `details` and `meta` fields — `details` is an empty string and `meta` is undefined, despite the operation name and reason being available at construction time.

---

Original implementation from [#440](https://github.com/withastro/flue/pull/440) by @hiro-nikaitou

title: fix(runtime): preserve structured operation and reason in OperationFailedError
body:
## Problem

`OperationFailedError` hardcodes `details: ''` and omits `meta`, so the serialized error on a failed dispatched operation contains no structured data. Downstream error trackers must regex-parse the prose message to recover the operation name and underlying reason, which breaks issue grouping (the embedded dispatch UUID makes every occurrence a unique message) and prevents programmatic classification.

Closes #431.

## Changes

`packages/runtime/src/errors.ts` — two changes in `OperationFailedError`:

1. **`details`** is now populated with `reason` instead of `''`, so callers receive the underlying failure text as structured detail rather than having to extract it from the prose message.
2. **`meta`** now carries `{ operation, reason }`, matching the pattern used by other `FlueError` subclasses (e.g. `CloudflareAIBindingError`, `AttachmentLoadingError`).

## Verification

title: Persistent agents: submission-scoped abort — instance-wide POST /abort is the only external cancellation primitive and cancels unrelated queued/in-flight work
body:
## Context

Same production setup as #426/#425: a persistent per-case support agent whose Durable Object instance serves several kinds of work concurrently — dispatched draft-generation runs, operator chat turns queued into the shared conversation, and secondary dispatched jobs (duplicate-summary notes).

We recently started ending the draft dispatch as soon as its terminal result is durably persisted on our side: everything after that point (the child task's final report and the parent's closing message) is narration that costs ~2 model turns per draft and adds nothing the operator sees. The natural implementation is "abort the dispatch once the result is safe".

## Problem

The only external cancellation primitive is the instance-wide `POST /agents/:name/:id/abort` (`src/cloudflare/agent-coordinator.ts` — `isAbortRequest` → `abortInstance`), which `requestSessionAbort`s the whole submission session and aborts every active controller. Used on this hot per-draft path it cancels collateral work:

- queued/in-flight operator chat turns on the same conversation die silently mid-answer;
- concurrent duplicate-summary dispatches are killed and surface as operator-visible failures;
- a replacement draft dispatch admitted in the window between our settle and the abort landing gets killed and reconciles as a spurious failure.

`abortInstance` is the right shape for true drains (supersede storms, admin reset — the #426 mitigation), but there is no way to end *one* submission from outside. The node coordinator (`src/node/agent-coordinator.ts`) has the same session-wide-only shape.

## Ask

A submission-scoped abort route, mirroring `abortInstance` semantics for a single submission:

```
POST /agents/:name/:id/submissions/:submissionId/abort  →  { aborted: boolean }
```

- run store: `requestSubmissionAbort(sessionKey, submissionId)` — the existing `requestSessionAbort` (`src/sql-run-store.ts`) with a `AND submission_id = ?` scope, same `abort_requested_at = COALESCE(...)` stamp;
- coordinator: abort the matching active controller, arm the submission wake, reconcile — identical to `abortInstance` minus the loop;
- route matcher by exact tail position (like `isAbortRequest`) so agent/instance names cannot misroute.

The durable `abortRequestedAt` + reconcile fallback already settles aborted submissions individually (that is how a session abort settles each affected submission today), so the change is additive and small — no new settlement semantics.

## Workaround

We are running a local pnpm patch on the vendored runtime implementing exactly the above (coordinator `abortSubmission`, store `requestSubmissionAbort`, tail-position route matcher), verified in production use for post-persist run termination. Happy to send a PR — it mirrors `abortInstance` line-for-line. Would love this in `1.0.0-beta.10` so the patch drops with the repin.

title: Forward record envelope timestamps onto conversation stream chunks

labels.name: fix pending
labels.description: Fixed on a development branch; lands with the next release

body:
## Motivation

Diagnostic/audit consumers of the `updates` view need to reconstruct run chronology from the chunk stream. Today only `message-started` (`timestamp`) and `message-appended` (`message.metadata.timestamp`) carry a server-authored time; `tool-input`, `tool-output`, `tool-output-error`, `message-delta`, `message-completed`, and `submission-settled` chunks carry none.

The capture-time truth already exists: every canonical record carries `ConversationRecordEnvelope.timestamp` (`packages/runtime/src/conversation-records.ts`). The projection in `packages/runtime/src/conversation-public.ts` (`projectRecordToChunks`) simply does not forward it for those chunk types.

Concrete impact: we rebuild a diagnostic timeline from the updates view for operator debugging. A ~90s agent run projects to chunks whose only usable anchors are per-message start times, so tool execution boundaries and settlement times have to be labeled as estimates in the export instead of recorded facts.

## Request

Forward the record envelope `timestamp` onto the projected chunk for:

- `tool-input` (from `assistant_tool_call`)
- `tool-output` / `tool-output-error` (from the `tool_outcome` record)
- `message-completed` (from `assistant_message_completed`)
- `submission-settled` (from `submission_settled`)

An optional `timestamp?: string` field keeps the change additive and wire-compatible with existing consumers.

`message-delta` is deliberately listed separately: per-delta stamps add real wire weight for a field chat UIs never render. Fine to leave deltas out — consumers can interpolate between the surrounding stamped chunks once the boundaries above are stamped.

## Alternative considered

Reading the canonical record stream directly instead of the updates view — but #407 established the updates view as the supported surface for attached-agent consumers, so the projection is where the fidelity should live.
