title: feat(sdk): add reasoning effort option to prompt/skill/task
body:
# Add `reasoning` option to `prompt()`, `skill()`, `task()`, `init()`, and role frontmatter

## Why this PR

Closes a small gap between `pi-ai` and Flue:

- `pi-ai` already supports `SimpleStreamOptions.reasoning` across every
  reasoning-capable provider (Anthropic, OpenAI Completions/Responses,
  Google, Google Vertex, Azure, Bedrock, Mistral, OpenRouter, …). Each
  provider clamps the requested level against `Model.thinkingLevelMap`.
- `pi-agent-core` already exposes `state.thinkingLevel` and forwards it as
  `SimpleStreamOptions.reasoning` on every stream call
  (`agent.js:createLoopConfig`).
- Flue surfaces neither. Today, reasoning effort is fixed per model in the
  registry, so serving N tiers (e.g. a cheap classifier at `low`, a careful
  auditor at `xhigh`) from one deployment requires N model entries or N
  deployments.

This PR wires the existing underlying capability onto Flue's public surface
so a single agent can pick effort per call.

## Motivation

The use case that drove this: orchestration systems that call the same
model with different depth-of-thought depending on the task, without
multiplying deployments. With this change, an agent can route cheap work
to `low` and critical audits to `xhigh` on the same model, in the same
session, with no additional infra.

## API

```ts
const agent = await init({
  model: 'anthropic/claude-opus-4-7',
  reasoning: 'medium', // default for every call
});
const session = await agent.session();

await session.prompt('Summarize this thread.');                    // medium
await session.prompt('Audit this diff.', { reasoning: 'xhigh' });  // xhigh
await session.task('Research this library.', { reasoning: 'high' });
```

Role files pick up `reasoning:` from frontmatter:

```md
---
model: anthropic/claude-opus-4-7
reasoning: high
---
```

## Precedence

`call > role > session > agent` — identical to `model`.

## Validation

- Passing `reasoning` against a model whose pi-ai metadata reports
  `reasoning: false` throws a `[flue]`-prefixed runtime `Error` naming the
  field and the model (no dedicated error class — aligns with how the rest
  of the SDK surfaces config errors).
- `'off'` is valid only at init / role / session tiers. Passing it per-call
  throws; per-call code should pick a concrete effort or omit the option
  entirely.
- Unknown levels in role frontmatter throw at build time.
- pi-ai's `clampThinkingLevel` silently maps unsupported levels (e.g.
  `xhigh` on a model without that mapping) to the closest supported one.
  Flue does not intercept that.

## Forwarding

The resolved level is written to `harness.state.thinkingLevel` before each
prompt / skill / task call and restored on exit, including on validation
failure (the harness's previous state is never mutated until every resolve
succeeds). pi-agent-core then maps the level to `SimpleStreamOptions.reasoning`
on every stream call.

### Minor refactor inside `withScopedRuntime`

Adding strict validation meant `resolveThinkingLevelForCall` can now throw
from the middle of the scoped-runtime setup. In the pre-existing code, the
harness state (`model`, `systemPrompt`, `tools`) was mutated as each value
was resolved, so a throw between mutations left the harness half-updated
and the `try/finally` never ran (the throw happened before the `try`).
That would have been a regression introduced by this PR.

The fix is local and mechanical: resolve every value into local variables
first, then capture `previous*` snapshots, then mutate all four
`state.*` fields together, then enter the `try { ... } finally { restore }`
block. Same variables (`previousTools`, `previousModel`,
`previousSystemPrompt`), same restore logic, same number of
`this.harness.state.*` accesses — just reordered so the mutation is
atomic. A test (`'leaves harness state intact when reasoning validation
fails'`) pins the rollback contract.

If you'd prefer the refactor to land as a separate commit or a follow-up
PR, happy to split it out.

## Compaction

Compaction has its own default of `'high'` when the model supports reasoning
(keeps summary quality, which feeds every future turn). Setting
`reasoning: 'off'` at the agent level also disables reasoning inside
compaction. Any other agent-level value leaves compaction at its default —
per-call / role / session reasoning intentionally does not propagate to
compaction, because that's internal work driven by agent config, not the
current user call.

## Tests

37 tests across three files (`pnpm run test` from `packages/sdk/`):

- `test/reasoning.test.ts` — unit tests for `resolveCallReasoning` and
  `parseReasoningFrontmatter` (precedence, `"off"` semantics, validation,
  frontmatter parsing).
- `test/reasoning-forwarding.test.ts` — integration tests with a fake
  `streamFn` capturing `SimpleStreamOptions` for `prompt()`, `skill()`, and
  `task()`; covers role × session × agent precedence on the wire, harness
  state rollback on validation failure, and session-reasoning inheritance
  across nested task sessions.
- `test/compaction-reasoning.test.ts` — semantic mirror + source-text anchor
  for the compaction reasoning branch.

## Out of scope

- `thinkingBudgets` (Anthropic/Gemini token-based budgets) — follow-up.
- Vercel AI Gateway / OpenRouter-specific routing knobs — follow-up.
- Provider auto-fallback beyond pi-ai's `clampThinkingLevel` — keeping
  strict for now.
- HTTP body snapshot of the outgoing Responses API request — would require
  exposing a mockable base-URL harness; the `streamFn`-level tests cover
  the SDK boundary.

## Notes for the maintainer

- Positional parameters on `createBuiltinTools` (6) and `runTaskForTool`
  (7) grew with this PR. A context-object refactor makes sense the next
  time those signatures are touched; deferred here to keep the diff
  focused.
- The test runner uses a small in-process harness (`test/run.ts`) because
  Node 22's `--test` flag combined with `--experimental-transform-types`
  silently drops `describe` blocks when the file transitively imports code
  using TS parameter properties (observed with `src/result.ts`). Running
  the suite in-process sidesteps the subprocess isolation bug. Happy to
  switch to a different runner (tsx, vitest) if you prefer.
- No Changeset file because the repo doesn't use `@changesets/cli` — all
  the release notes content lives here in the PR body.

title: `flue run` terminates long-running local agents after ~300s of no SSE events
S3-compatible virtual sandbox alongside the R2 one?
body:
Hi, I'd like to write a generic S3 adapter for our users (I work at Tigris data).

`@flue/sdk/cloudflare#getVirtualSandbox`(R2) is great if you're on Cloudflare. 
However, there's no equivalent for Node, GitHub Actions, Workers without an R2 binding, or buckets that aren't R2.
The virtual sandbox falls back to in-memory and the agent forgets everything between calls.

I'd like to add `@flue/sdk/s3#getS3Sandbox`. It is the same BashFactory shape as the existing one, generic over any S3-compatible endpoint (AWS, Tigris, MinIO, R2's S3 API). `@aws-sdk/client-s3` as an optional peer dep, the way wrangler is today. Lazy-imported, so projects that don't use it pay nothing.

Happy to share the implementation if it'd help you decide.

Dave

title: Support StandardSchema + StandardJSONSchema for result instead of only Valibot
body:
## Problem
Internally, Flue calls `toJsonSchema` from Valibot's library (`@valibot/to-json-schema`). This forces the consumer to install Valibot as a dependency in their project even if they have an existing validation lib.

## Suggestion
I think Flue should allow users to use any validation library they want by implementing the `StandardJSONSchema` & `StandardSchema` interface for the `result` object instead.

### Benefits
- `flue/sdk` reduces 2 runtime deps.
- Allows users to use any lib that uses Standard Schema / Standard JSON Schema. They can reuse their existing validation lib, no extra dependency.

## Breaking Changes
- Existing Valibot users will encounter errors on upgrade. They need to install `@valibot/to-json-schema` in their own project and explicitly call `toStandardJsonSchema` in their agent.
------

If this is a welcome change, I'd be happy to look into it and create a PR. 

PS: Loving Flue so far! Super clean abstractions, I think a framework for building agents is exactly what is needed now.

title: add boxd connector instructions
body: ## Summary - Adds `connectors/sandbox--boxd.md` alongside the existing Daytona and Vercel connectors. Slug `boxd`, alias `@boxd-sh/sdk`, website https://boxd.sh. - Mirrors the existing connector shape: wraps an already-initialized `Box` from `@boxd-sh/sdk` into a `SandboxFactory`. `cleanup: true` calls `box.destroy()` on session end; the user owns the rest of the VM lifecycle. - Adds a working example in `examples/hello-world/` matching the Daytona pattern (`.flue/connectors/boxd.ts` + `.flue/agents/with-boxd.ts`). ## Why boxd boxd ships microVMs over a `Compute` / `Box` SDK that's already on npm at `@boxd-sh/sdk`. Cold start is sub-second and forks land in milliseconds, which fits the same niche as Daytona and Vercel Sandbox. Flue users who want a real Linux VM per agent session now have one more drop-in option. ## Implementation notes - `box.exec()` takes argv and has no native `cwd` option, so all `SandboxApi` calls route through `bash -lc`, prepending `cd ` when one is supplied. Same approach the Vercel connector uses for shell wrapping. - `stat` / `readdir` / `mkdir` / `rm` / `exists` shell out, matching the way the Daytona connector falls back to `exec('mkdir -p ...')` for recursive mkdir. The boxd SDK doesn't expose those operations directly today. - `timeout` is converted from seconds (Flue spec) to milliseconds (boxd SDK). - Auth: `BOXD_API_KEY` (preferred) or `BOXD_TOKEN`. The connector instructions tell the agent never to invent values, same wording as the other connectors. ## Two boxd-specific quirks the connector handles transparently These were caught during end-to-end testing against a real boxd VM: 1. **Default cwd is `/home/boxd`**, not `/root`. boxd VMs run as user `boxd` and `cd /root` fails with "Permission denied". 2. **`c.box.create()` returns before the in-VM exec endpoint is up.** First exec hits `ConnectionError: connection refused`. The connector polls `box.exec(['true'])` once per box (result cached across sessions) before the first user-facing exec. Configurable via `readyTimeoutMs`, default 30s, set to 0 to skip on warm boxes. ## Verification - `pnpm install && pnpm --filter @flue/sdk run build && pnpm --filter @flue/cli run build` regenerates `_connectors.generated.ts` with three entries (`boxd`, `daytona`, `vercel`). - `node packages/cli/dist/flue.js add` lists `boxd` correctly under "Available connectors". - The connector TypeScript body typechecks cleanly against the real `@flue/sdk/sandbox` exports and `@boxd-sh/sdk@0.1.2` types (`tsc --noEmit`, `--strict`). - End-to-end, against a real boxd production VM via the example agent (`flue run with-boxd`): ``` [boxd] created box: flue-test-1778009548011 → flue-test-1778009548011.boxd.sh [boxd] uname: Linux flue-test-... GNU/Linux [boxd] file round-trip: PASS [boxd] compound: PASS [boxd] pipe: PASS [boxd] find|wc: PASS [boxd] ALL PASSED ``` ## Test plan - [x] `pnpm --filter @flue/cli build` — frontmatter validates and the index regenerates with three connectors. - [x] `flue add` lists `boxd`. - [x] End-to-end: agent uses connector → boxd VM → shell ops succeed → cleanup destroys the box. - [ ] After website rebuild on merge, `https://flueframework.com/cli/connectors/boxd.md` serves the body without frontmatter. - [ ] `flue add boxd | claude` (or another agent) installs the connector verbatim into a fresh project. ## Notes for review Drafting this since the upstream maintainers haven't seen the boxd SDK before. Happy to drop the example agent + connector copy if you'd prefer to match the Vercel precedent (markdown-only). The hero image lives under `pr-assets/` matching what we did for the Hermes contribution; feel free to ask us to remove it before merge.

title: add boxd connector instructions
body:
## Summary

- Adds a `sandbox--boxd.md` connector at the top-level `connectors/` directory, alongside `sandbox--daytona.md` and `sandbox--vercel.md`.
- Slug: `boxd`. Alias: `@boxd-sh/sdk`. Website: https://boxd.sh.
- Follows the same shape as the existing Daytona and Vercel connectors: the connector wraps an already-initialized `Box` from `@boxd-sh/sdk` into a `SandboxFactory`. Optional `cleanup: true` calls `box.destroy()` when the session ends; the user owns the rest of the VM lifecycle.

## Why boxd

boxd ships microVMs (sub-second cold start, fork in ~milliseconds) over a `Compute` / `Box` SDK that's already on npm at `@boxd-sh/sdk`. It fits the same niche as Daytona and Vercel Sandbox in the existing connector roster, so users who want a real Linux VM per agent session have one more drop-in option.

## Implementation notes

- `box.exec()` takes argv and has no native `cwd` option, so all `SandboxApi` calls route through `bash -lc`, prepending `cd <cwd>` when one is supplied. Same approach the Vercel connector uses for shell wrapping.
- `stat` / `readdir` / `mkdir` / `rm` / `exists` shell out, the way the Daytona connector falls back to `exec('mkdir -p ...')` for recursive mkdir. The boxd SDK doesn't expose those operations directly today.
- `timeout` is converted from seconds (Flue spec) to milliseconds (boxd SDK).
- Auth: `BOXD_API_KEY` (preferred) or `BOXD_TOKEN`. The connector instructions tell the agent never to invent values, same wording as the other connectors.

## Verification

- `pnpm install && pnpm --filter @flue/sdk run build && pnpm --filter @flue/cli run build` regenerates `_connectors.generated.ts` with three entries (`boxd`, `daytona`, `vercel`).
- `node packages/cli/dist/flue.js add` lists `boxd` correctly under `Available connectors`.
- The connector's TypeScript body typechecks cleanly against the real `@flue/sdk/sandbox` exports and `@boxd-sh/sdk@0.1.2` types (`tsc --noEmit`, strict).

## Test plan

- [ ] `pnpm --filter @flue/cli build` — frontmatter validates and the index regenerates with three connectors.
- [ ] `flue add` — `boxd` shows up in the listing.
- [ ] After the website rebuild, `https://flueframework.com/cli/connectors/boxd.md` serves the body without frontmatter.
- [ ] End-to-end: pipe `flue add boxd` to a coding agent in a sample project, confirm it writes a working `connectors/boxd.ts` and that `flue dev` runs an agent against a real boxd VM.

title: Sandbox connector cleanup: `cleanup: true` doesn't fire automatically
body:
## Problem

Sandbox connectors (Daytona, future ones) accept a `cleanup: true` option that, by name and by docs, should delete the underlying sandbox when the request finishes. Today it only fires when something calls `agent.destroy()` — and nothing in the runtime ever calls that. So a webhook agent like:

\`\`\`typescript
export default async function ({ init, env }: FlueContext) {
  const client = new Daytona({ apiKey: env.DAYTONA_API_KEY });
  const sandbox = await client.create();

  const agent = await init({
    sandbox: daytona(sandbox, { cleanup: true }),
    model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6',
  });
  const session = await agent.session();

  return await session.shell('uname -a');
}
\`\`\`

…leaks a Daytona sandbox per request. The current docs (#42) accurately describe `cleanup: true` as it *should* work. We just need to make the runtime match the docs.

## Discovered via

[withastro/flue#42](https://github.com/withastro/flue/pull/42) — @mu-hashmi tested this against a real Daytona project and confirmed the leak. We considered documenting `try/finally { await agent.destroy() }` as the workaround, but the wrapping is ugly and the user shouldn't have to know about `destroy()` at all for the common case.

## Affected today

- `cleanup: true` in `examples/hello-world/.flue/connectors/daytona.ts` — fires only on `destroy()`.
- `examples/hello-world/.flue/agents/with-sandbox.ts` — leaks a sandbox per test run.
- Anyone copy-pasting from \`docs/connect-daytona.md\`.

## Proposed fix — two candidate APIs

### Option A: runtime auto-destroys agents created via \`init()\`

The Node webhook adapter and Cloudflare DO handler already wrap the user's agent function. After the handler returns or throws, call \`destroy()\` on every \`FlueAgent\` instance created in that request.

- Pro: zero user code, matches the docs we already shipped.
- Pro: handles the shared-sandbox case correctly — \`cleanup: true\` on any one of N agents that share a sandbox still fires once, after the request.
- Con: implicit. A user who holds onto an \`agent\` reference past the request boundary (e.g. stashed on a global) will see it get destroyed underneath them. Probably fine — that's not a pattern we want to support anyway — but worth calling out.

### Option B: \`ctx.defer(fn)\` on \`FlueContext\` (mirrors \`ctx.waitUntil\`)

Expose a \`defer\` (or similarly named) hook on the context that runs registered functions after the handler resolves, regardless of throw/return. Connectors call it internally when \`cleanup: true\`; users can call it directly for any cleanup.

- Pro: general primitive. Useful beyond sandboxes — DB connection cleanup, analytics flush, etc.
- Pro: explicit. Easy to reason about lifecycle.
- Con: connectors now need access to the context. Currently \`SandboxFactory.createSessionEnv\` doesn't get one.

## Recommendation

Probably both, in order: ship Option A first because it makes the existing docs true, then add Option B as a public primitive when we hit a second use case (we will).

## Out of scope for this issue

- \`Symbol.asyncDispose\` / \`using\` syntax — nice future ergonomics, but doesn't help users who don't want to touch the lifecycle at all.
- Connector cleanup running on \`session\` close vs \`agent\` close — keep it agent-scoped, that's where the lifecycle parallel makes sense.

title: [HIGH] Unauthenticated webhook endpoints allow arbitrary remote agent execution and session continuation by URL id
body: **Affected area** Generated HTTP server paths for both Node and Cloudflare targets `(/agents/:name/:id)`. Flue-generated webhook routes accept `POST /agents/:name/:id` requests without any built-in authentication or authorization requirement. As a result, any network caller who can reach the endpoint can invoke agent handlers. Because session identity is keyed by URL` :id`, a caller can also continue existing stateful sessions if they know/guess that id. **Why this is a security issue** This creates two concrete risks: 1. Arbitrary remote execution of agent logic Any unauthenticated caller can trigger business logic, tool usage, shell execution (if enabled by app), and downstream API calls. 2. Session hijack / state manipulation by id reuse Stateful behavior can be continued or overwritten by a second caller reusing the same `:id`, enabling cross-actor session interference. **Impact** - Unauthorized access to protected agent capabilities. - Unauthorized mutation of session state. - Potential data leakage in responses/events/history. - Abuse risk and cost amplification (model/tool calls). - Potential lateral impact depending on app-specific tools/commands configured by developers. **Exploitability** Low complexity: - Requires only network access to the endpoint. - No credential needed. - No protocol bypass needed; standard `POST` is sufficient. **Observed behavior** - Request accepted with only JSON body. - No auth header/cookie/token check required. - Same `:id` from different callers continues shared state. **Expected behavior** At framework level, public webhook invocation should be fail-closed by default unless the developer explicitly configures authentication bypass. Session continuity should not be exposed to arbitrary callers by default. **Scope / assumptions** - This is framework-level behavior, not a misconfiguration in a single app. - Even if some users place Flue behind external auth proxies, secure defaults should still exist in the SDK/CLI generated runtime.

title: Docs should mention prompt injection.
body:
## Context

The existing security guidance in the deploy docs is missing any guidance around **prompt injection**.  Specifically, untrusted input steering a tool-using agent into doing the wrong thing on the developer's behalf. 

Given the patterns Flue is actively showcasing, I think this deserves explicit treatment.
## Why it matters here

The support-agent example in the README and Cloudflare docs is essentially the textbook ["lethal trifecta"](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/):

1. **Untrusted input** — webhook trigger, end-user content lands directly in the prompt
2. **Private data access** — R2 knowledge base mounted as the agent's filesystem, accessible via `grep` / `read` / `glob`
3. **Exfiltration channel** — virtual sandbox with bash and network reachability

None of this is unique to Flue. The concern is that Flue's defaults make it unusually easy to land in this configuration without realizing it, because the framework's value prop is exactly "wire these things together quickly."

## What could help

A section in deployment documentation: 

- Names prompt injection as a concern distinct from sandbox escape / secret leakage 
- Calls out the trust boundary on webhook payloads and on any mounted R2 / filesystem content the agent can read
- Sketches mitigation patterns for the support-agent-style use case, e.g. constraining tool surface per session, validating outputs beyond shape (the valibot `result` schema pins response shape but not the agent's behavior during the run), human-in-the-loop on side-effecting tools, separating "read untrusted input" agents from "act on private data" agents
- If there are framework-level hooks for guardrails / output filtering / tool-call gating, link to them prominently; if there aren't, surfacing that limitation in the docs is itself useful signal for people evaluating Flue for production

title: List of bugs/incorrect behavior
body:
(from claude code)

## Summary

Several current Flue issues can cause leaked processes, silently missing HTTP routes, broken generated builds, and misleading agent tool behavior. These are the highest-impact verified problems to fix first.

## Issues

### 1. `flue run` does not wire spawned server into signal cleanup

`packages/cli/bin/flue.ts` declares a global `serverProcess` for signal cleanup:

- `serverProcess` is declared at `packages/cli/bin/flue.ts:996`
- SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers call `stopServer(serverProcess)` at `packages/cli/bin/flue.ts:998-1005`
- `run()` starts the server as a local `const child` at `packages/cli/bin/flue.ts:721`

Because `child` is never assigned to `serverProcess`, the signal cleanup path is effectively dead code. Normal completion calls `stopServer(child)`, but parent-only termination can leak the spawned Node server process and leave the port occupied.

Suggested fix: assign the spawned child to `serverProcess` and clear it after cleanup.

---

### 2. `parseTriggers()` is regex-parsing live TypeScript

`packages/sdk/src/build.ts:278-296` extracts triggers with regex:

```ts
const triggersExportMatch = source.match(/export\s+const\s+triggers\s*=\s*\{([^}]*)\}/);
```

This silently fails or mis-parses valid code, for example:

```ts
export const triggers: Triggers = { webhook: true };
```

The type annotation causes the regex to miss the export entirely, so the agent becomes trigger-less and gets no HTTP route.

Other failure modes:

```ts
export const triggers = { webhook: true, options: { foo: 1 } };
```

The capture stops at the first `}`.

```ts
export const triggers = {
  // cron: '0 0 * * *'
};
```

The cron regex can match commented-out code.

This directly controls whether agents are exposed over HTTP via `agents.filter((a) => a.triggers.webhook)` in `packages/sdk/src/build.ts:54`.

Suggested fix: parse the file with a TypeScript AST or another real parser, and fail loudly on unsupported trigger declarations.

---

### 3. Agent filename normalization can collide or break generated output

Both build targets generate JS identifiers by flattening non-alphanumeric chars:

- Node: `packages/sdk/src/build-plugin-node.ts:290-292`
- Cloudflare: `packages/sdk/src/build-plugin-cloudflare.ts:596-598`

```ts
function agentVarName(name: string): string {
  return 'handler_' + name.replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9]/g, '_');
}
```

This means these two agents collide:

```txt
agents/hello-world.ts
agents/hello_world.ts
```

Both become `handler_hello_world`, producing duplicate imports in generated code.

Cloudflare also has a route mismatch for camelCase agent names:

- `agentClassName()` only splits on `-` and `_` at `packages/sdk/src/build-plugin-cloudflare.ts:607-611`
- `webhookAgentNames` stores raw filenames at `packages/sdk/src/build-plugin-cloudflare.ts:134`
- The worker precheck compares the URL name against those raw names at `packages/sdk/src/build-plugin-cloudflare.ts:470`

For an agent like `agents/myAgent.ts`, the Durable Object binding/routing path becomes kebab-cased by the `agents`/`partyserver` stack, while Flue's precheck still expects the raw filename.

Suggested fix: validate agent names during discovery and fail with a clear error for names that would collide or produce incompatible route/class names.

---

### 4. The `bash` tool throws on all non-zero exit codes

`packages/sdk/src/agent.ts:269-271` turns any non-zero exit into a tool error:

```ts
if (result.exitCode !== 0) {
  throw new Error(`${output}\n\nCommand exited with code ${result.exitCode}`);
}
```

Many shell commands use non-zero statuses for normal, useful outcomes:

- `grep` exits `1` when no matches are found
- `test` exits `1` for false
- `diff` exits `1` when files differ

The model should receive `{ stdout, stderr, exitCode }` and reason about it, not see a tool-level failure for expected command outcomes.

Suggested fix: return command output and exit code for all completed commands. Reserve thrown errors for execution failures, timeouts, or aborted commands.

---

### 5. The `glob` tool advertises recursive glob syntax but uses `find -name`

`packages/sdk/src/agent.ts:340-349` documents glob behavior:

```ts
description: 'Find files by glob pattern. Returns matching file paths.',
pattern: Type.String({ description: 'Glob pattern, e.g. "**/*.ts"' }),
```

But implementation uses:

```ts
find ${escapeShellArg(searchPath)} -type f -name "${escapeShellArg(params.pattern)}"
```

`find -name` matches a single pathname component. It does not implement `**/*.ts` recursive glob semantics, so the documented example returns no results.

Suggested fix: use a real glob implementation, or change the tool contract/description to match `find -name` behavior.

---

### 6. Grep/glob shell commands do not quote `searchPath`

`packages/sdk/src/agent.ts:298`, `300`, and `349` escape `searchPath` but do not shell-quote it:

```ts
grep -rn "${escapeShellArg(params.pattern)}" ${escapeShellArg(searchPath)}
find ${escapeShellArg(searchPath)} -type f ...
```

`escapeShellArg()` only escapes `\`, `"`, `$`, and `` ` `` at `packages/sdk/src/agent.ts:391-392`; it does not wrap the argument in quotes.

A path like:

```txt
/Users/Foo Bar/project
```

word-splits into multiple shell arguments.

Suggested fix: use proper shell argument quoting for both patterns and paths, or avoid shell string construction where practical.

---

### 7. Overflow recovery only works once per live session

`packages/sdk/src/session.ts:139` defines:

```ts
private overflowRecoveryAttempted = false;
```

On overflow, it is set to true at `packages/sdk/src/session.ts:766-768`:

```ts
if (this.overflowRecoveryAttempted) return;
this.overflowRecoveryAttempted = true;
```

It is never reset after successful compaction/retry in `runCompaction()` (`packages/sdk/src/session.ts:797-884`).

That means a long-lived session can recover from one context overflow, but a second overflow in the same live session will not attempt recovery.

Suggested fix: reset `overflowRecoveryAttempted` after successful overflow compaction and retry.

## Suggested fix order

1. Wire `serverProcess` in `flue run`.
2. Change the `bash` tool to return non-zero exit codes instead of throwing.
3. Replace regex trigger parsing with a real parser or a strict validated format.
4. Fix `glob` semantics and quote grep/glob paths correctly.
5. Validate agent filenames during discovery to catch collisions and Cloudflare route incompatibilities early.
6. Reset overflow recovery state after successful recovery.

title: Add a supported way to stop running prompts
body:
## Summary

Flue should provide a supported way to stop a running prompt without deleting the session or losing conversation history.

## Current Behavior

If an agent prompt is running for a long time, there does not seem to be a public API to cancel just that run.

`session.delete()` can stop work indirectly, but it also deletes session state, which is not ideal.

## Expected Behavior

There should be a clean cancellation API for running prompts.

Ideally, Flue would support `AbortSignal` in prompt calls:

```ts
const controller = new AbortController();

await session.prompt("Do some work", {
  signal: controller.signal,
});

controller.abort();
```

This would let apps build reliable “Stop” buttons in their UI.

## HTTP / Streaming Use Case

For streamed responses, it would also be useful to expose a run ID and provide an abort endpoint, for example:

```txt
POST /agents/<agent-name>/<agent-id>/runs/<run-id>/abort
```

That endpoint could cancel the running prompt while preserving the session.

## Why This Matters

A supported abort mechanism would help users:

- stop accidental or expensive long-running prompts
- cancel work from a UI button
- keep session history intact
- avoid killing the whole server or deleting the session
- build better streaming agent interfaces

## Request

Please add first-class prompt cancellation support, preferably using `AbortSignal` as the core API, with an HTTP abort endpoint built on top for streamed/remote runs.

## Contribution

If this sounds useful and the maintainers agree with the direction, I’m happy to open a PR for it.

Would an `AbortSignal`-based API plus a run-based HTTP abort endpoint be an acceptable approach?

title: Show model thinking in streaming responses
body:
## Summary

Flue supports streaming responses, but it does not currently seem to stream model thinking or reasoning output.

## What I Expected

When using a model that supports thinking or reasoning, I expected the streaming response to include those thinking updates, similar to how it streams normal text output and tool events.

## What Happens Today

The stream includes normal assistant text and tool activity, but not thinking or reasoning updates.

This makes it hard to build UIs that show what the agent is doing while it is reasoning, especially for longer-running agent tasks.

## Why This Would Be Useful

Showing thinking or reasoning updates would help users understand:

- whether the agent is still actively working
- what phase of reasoning it is in
- why a long-running response is taking time
- what is happening before tools are called or final text is produced

## Request

Please expose thinking or reasoning events in the streaming API when the underlying model or provider supports them.

It would also be useful to have a public option for enabling or configuring thinking level, for example off, minimal, low, medium, or high.

title: Expose Dynamic Provider Auth Hook For Flue `session.prompt()`
body:
Flue currently resolves models by provider/model id and runs LLM work through `session.prompt()`, `session.skill()`, and `session.task()`, but the SDK does not expose pi-agent-core's dynamic `getApiKey(provider)` hook to Flue agent authors.

This blocks OAuth-backed providers whose access tokens are resolved or refreshed at runtime, such as OpenAI Codex / ChatGPT OAuth via `@mariozechner/pi-ai`.

## User-Visible Symptom

`openai-codex/gpt-5.3-codex` could be called through `pi-ai` directly, but not through Flue's normal `session.prompt()` path using local OAuth credentials.

The first working smoke had to call `pi-ai complete()` directly from the Flue handler. That meant the actual LLM completion bypassed Flue's session abstraction.

## Expected Behavior
Flue should allow an agent to provide a dynamic credential resolver:

```ts
const agent = await init({
  model: "openai-codex/gpt-5.3-codex",
  getApiKey: async (provider) => {
    if (provider !== "openai-codex") return undefined;
    return resolveOAuthAccessTokenSomehow();
  },
});

const session = await agent.session();
const result = await session.prompt("...", { result: SomeSchema });
```

The prompt should still run through Flue:

- session history
- roles
- skills
- tools
- task orchestration
- result extraction
- compaction

## Actual Behavior

Without a Flue-level auth hook, the only practical options are:

- rely on provider environment variables, which does not fit OAuth token refresh flows,
- bypass Flue and call `pi-ai` directly,
- fork/patch internal runtime behavior without a typed SDK surface.

## Evidence

pi-agent-core already supports the needed abstraction:

- `AgentOptions.getApiKey?: (provider: string) => Promise<string | undefined> | string | undefined`
- The agent loop resolves credentials at the LLM boundary using the model provider.

`pi-ai` already supports programmatic OAuth token resolution:

- `getOAuthApiKey(provider, credentials)` returns an API key and refreshed credentials.

OpenClaw upstream documents OpenAI Codex OAuth as supported for external workflows and describes runtime refresh/expiry behavior.

## Proposed Fix

Add a provider-agnostic resolver to Flue:

```ts
export type ApiKeyResolver =
  (provider: string) => Promise<string | undefined> | string | undefined;

export interface AgentInit {
  getApiKey?: ApiKeyResolver;
}
```

Then:

- propagate it through `createFlueContext()`,
- store it in `AgentConfig`,
- pass it into pi-agent-core `new Agent({ getApiKey })`,
- use it for compaction calls as well.

title: No way to configure provider baseUrl/headers for enterprise API gateways
body:
## Problem

When deploying Flue agents in enterprise environments, LLM traffic is typically routed through an API gateway or proxy (e.g. Azure APIM, internal Anthropic-compatible proxies). These require:

- A custom `baseUrl` (e.g. `https://enterprise-proxy.example.com/anthropic`)
- One or more custom request headers for authentication (e.g. `Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key`, `X-Custom-Auth`)

Flue resolves models through `@mariozechner/pi-ai`'s built-in static registry (`models.generated.js`). That registry has hardcoded provider endpoints with no `baseUrl` or `headers` set. There is currently no way to override these through `init()` or any other Flue API.

## What Pi's ModelRegistry does (the right pattern already exists)

The Oh My Pi coding harness solves this via `~/.omp/agent/models.yml`:

```yaml
providers:
  anthropic:
    baseUrl: https://enterprise-proxy.example.com/anthropic
    headers:
      X-Custom-Auth: <token>
    apiKey: dummy
    disableStrictTools: true
```

`ModelRegistry` applies these overrides to the built-in model objects at startup (step 3 of its merge pipeline), so `model.baseUrl` and `model.headers` are set by the time the Anthropic client is constructed. Flue agents running standalone never go through `ModelRegistry`, so those overrides are lost.

## Workarounds tried (both fragile)

**1. Mutate the model registry directly** — import `getModel` from `@mariozechner/pi-ai` and patch `model.baseUrl`/`model.headers` before `init()`. Works only if the bundler does not inline `@mariozechner/pi-ai` as a separate copy from what Flue's internal code uses. Undocumented, breaks on bundler changes.

**2. Wrap `globalThis.fetch`** — intercept all fetch calls and inject the header for matching URLs. Works, but is a process-wide side effect at the wrong layer.

## Requested API

A `providers` option on `init()` that mirrors `models.yml` provider overrides:

```ts
const agent = await init({
  model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6',
  providers: {
    anthropic: {
      baseUrl: process.env.ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL,
      headers: {
        'X-Custom-Auth': process.env.GATEWAY_KEY,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

Alternatively, a top-level `configureProvider()` call at module init time would also work. The key requirement is that it flows into the `model.baseUrl` and `model.headers` fields that `@mariozechner/pi-ai`'s Anthropic provider already reads — so no new provider plumbing is needed, just a way to set those fields from user code.
