title: fix(sdk): honor bash tool timeout parameter end-to-end
body:
## Summary

The built-in `bash` tool already exposes a `timeout` parameter in its
JSON-Schema (in seconds), but `agent.ts` discards it with a `TODO`
comment. This PR threads `timeout` through `SessionEnv.exec` to the
adapters that actually consume it today — `@cloudflare/sandbox` and
Daytona — so an LLM-supplied timeout actually bounds the underlying
command on those platforms.

Just-bash (the default sandbox on Node) does not consume `timeout`
yet; this PR explicitly does NOT add structural plumbing for that
path. When just-bash gains support, a follow-up can extend the same
pattern.

## The bug

`packages/sdk/src/agent.ts:213` (current):

```ts
async execute(_toolCallId, params: { command: string; timeout?: number }, signal?) {
  throwIfAborted(signal);
  // TODO: wire timeout through SessionEnv.exec
  const result = await env.exec(params.command);
  return formatBashResult(result, params.command);
},
```

The schema declares `timeout` as `Type.Optional(Type.Number({ description: 'Timeout in seconds' }))`. An LLM supplying `{ command: '…long-running…', timeout: 30 }` is silently ignored. Hangs are user-visible as agents that never return.

## What changes

### Type surface

- `SessionEnv.exec` (`packages/sdk/src/types.ts`) — add `timeout?: number` (seconds) to the options bag.
- `SandboxApi.exec` (`packages/sdk/src/sandbox.ts`) — add `timeout?: number`. This is the contract remote sandbox adapters (CF Sandbox, Daytona) implement.
- `BashLike.exec` is **not** modified in this PR. The just-bash adapter
  strips `timeout` at its boundary so the field never reaches a runtime
  that wouldn't consume it.

### Adapter pass-through (units annotated)

```
   bash tool                ┌──────────────────────────────┐
   { timeout: 30 } ───────► │  SessionEnv.exec    (sec)    │
   (seconds)                └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                                           │
        ┌──────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┐
        ▼                                  ▼                                  ▼
  bashFactoryToSessionEnv         createSandboxSessionEnv             createCwdSessionEnv
   (strips `timeout` at the         (forwards on SandboxApi.exec)      (forwards to parent)
    just-bash boundary —
    just-bash ignores it today)
        │                                  │
        ▼                                  ▼
    bash.exec(cmd, {cwd,env})    SandboxApi.exec  (sec)
    no `timeout` passed                    │
                                ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                                ▼                     ▼
                       cfSandboxToSessionEnv      daytona connector
                       ┌─────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────────┐
                       │ sec → ms × 1000 │       │ passes seconds      │
                       └─────────┬───────┘       │ unchanged (caller   │
                                 ▼               │ wins; 120s fallback)│
                       @cloudflare/sandbox       └──────────┬──────────┘
                       BaseExecOptions.timeout              ▼
                       (ms)                       sandbox.process
                                                  .executeCommand(...)
                                                  (sec)
```

### Files touched

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `packages/sdk/src/types.ts` | + `timeout?: number` on `SessionEnv.exec` |
| `packages/sdk/src/sandbox.ts` | + `timeout?` on `SandboxApi`; pass through in `createSandboxSessionEnv` and `createCwdSessionEnv`; explicitly strip at the just-bash boundary in `createBashSessionEnv` |
| `packages/sdk/src/agent.ts` | bash tool: pass `params.timeout` into `env.exec`; runtime guard against NaN/Infinity/negative; `minimum: 0` in JSON-Schema; doc comment for the no-cap policy; remove `TODO` |
| `packages/sdk/src/cloudflare/cf-sandbox.ts` | propagate `timeout` to the CF Sandbox stub with a sec→ms conversion at the boundary |
| `packages/connectors/src/daytona.ts` | use caller-supplied `timeout`, fall back to existing 120s default |

## Design decisions

### Unit: seconds throughout

The bash tool's schema says "Timeout in seconds." `SessionEnv.exec`'s new
`timeout` keeps the same unit so there's no mental conversion at the
top of the call stack. Adapters that need milliseconds do the
multiplication at their boundary:

| Adapter | Native unit | Boundary handling |
|---------|-------------|-------------------|
| Just-bash (`bashFactoryToSessionEnv`) | does not consume `timeout` today | adapter strips the field; no leak |
| `@cloudflare/sandbox` (`cf-sandbox.ts`) | **milliseconds** (`BaseExecOptions.timeout`) | `seconds * 1000` at the adapter |
| Daytona (`packages/connectors/src/daytona.ts`) | seconds | passes through unchanged |

### Input validation

The bash tool's JSON-Schema declares `timeout` as `Type.Number({ minimum: 0 })`,
but LLMs can still emit `NaN`, `Infinity`, or negatives despite that
declaration. The tool guards at runtime: any non-finite or negative
value is treated as "caller did not supply a timeout" so the adapter's
default kicks in instead of being passed downstream.

### No SDK-level default cap

Flue does not impose a default upper bound. Rationale:

- CF Workers have their own request timeout that wins anyway.
- Daytona's connector already had a hardcoded 120s default; preserved as the fallback when no caller value is supplied.
- Just-bash today does not consume the field; once it does, host-level
  caps remain the host's policy.
- Adding a default in the SDK is policy that maintainers can layer on
  later without breaking this contract; the inverse is harder.

### Backwards compatibility

Every new field is optional. Existing callers that pass
`env.exec(cmd)` or `env.exec(cmd, { cwd, env })` continue to work
unchanged. `BashLike` is unmodified, so this PR has no surface area
against just-bash at all.

## Failure-mode coverage

```
                       ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
                       │  LLM emits bash tool call with       │
                       │     { command, timeout: N }          │
                       └────────────────┬─────────────────────┘
                                        │
                          ┌─────────────▼─────────────┐
                          │  Tool execute reads N     │   ← previously dropped
                          └─────────────┬─────────────┘
                                        ▼
                          ┌─────────────▼─────────────┐
                          │  SessionEnv.exec(cmd,     │
                          │    { timeout: N })        │
                          └─────────────┬─────────────┘
                                        ▼
                          ┌─────────────▼─────────────┐
                          │  Underlying runtime kills │
                          │  the process at N seconds │
                          └───────────────────────────┘
```

The "previously dropped" arrow is the bug; this PR removes that drop.

## Verification

```
pnpm install
pnpm check:types                   # passes; type changes flow through
pnpm --filter @flue/sdk build      # bundles cleanly
```

Type-check is the primary safety net here: the option-type addition flows
through every adapter, so a missed call site would surface as a TS error.
Behavioral verification is via the existing `examples/hello-world/` agents.

## Out of scope

- Adding a default cap in the SDK (see decision above).
- Modifying `BashLike.exec` or asking just-bash to honor `timeout`
  natively — that's an upstream conversation. This PR ships the
  observable behavior change on the adapters that consume `timeout`
  today; just-bash support can land alongside the just-bash version
  that adds it.
- Wiring `timeout` into `prompt()` / `skill()` / `task()` options. The
  shell-tool case is the highest-value single fix; per-call-level
  shell timeouts can follow.

title: test(sdk): add vitest infrastructure and unit tests for result.ts
body:
## Summary

Adds a minimal test runner setup (vitest) and a first unit-test file covering `packages/sdk/src/result.ts` — the structured-result extraction module.

The repo currently has zero unit tests; correctness is verified by example agents in `examples/hello-world/`, which need a real LLM API key to run. This PR provides a path for fast, deterministic, offline tests of pure-logic modules so future refactors can be done with safety nets.

## Motivation

`result.ts` is a good first target:

- Pure functions, no I/O, no LLM dependency.
- Real edge cases that bite in production: missing delimiters, multiple result blocks (last wins), malformed JSON, schema mismatch, half-open emissions, literal `---RESULT_END---` inside content.
- Tests pin the failure modes — we now have a regression suite for changes to the regex, the schema-rendering, the prompt assembly, and the error shape.

## What's in the PR

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `package.json` | + `vitest ^2.1.8` devDep, + root `test` script |
| `turbo.jsonc` | + `test` task (depends on `^build`, errors-only logs) |
| `packages/sdk/package.json` | + `test` / `test:watch` scripts |
| `packages/sdk/vitest.config.ts` | new — minimal config (4 lines) |
| `packages/sdk/src/result.test.ts` | new — 36 tests, all passing |

## Coverage of result.ts

- `extractResult`: object/array/string/number schemas, missing delimiters, multiple blocks (last wins), malformed JSON, schema mismatch, whitespace trimming, multi-line content, literal `---RESULT_END---` inside content (truncation behavior), half-open block, `rawOutput` carries trimmed block (not full input).
- `buildResultInstructions`: JSON Schema rendering for `v.object`, `v.array(v.object)`, `v.optional` (required-list semantics), `v.picklist` (enum).
- `buildResultExtractionPrompt`, `buildPromptText`, `buildSkillPrompt`: preamble exactly once, ordering (preamble → instructions → args → result delimiters), with/without schema, with/without args.
- `ResultExtractionError`: shape + `rawOutput` separate from `message`.

## Verification

```
pnpm install
pnpm --filter @flue/sdk test   # → 36/36 passing
pnpm test                       # → root via turbo: 3/3 tasks ok
pnpm check:types                # → unchanged, passes
```

## Why vitest?

- TypeScript-first, no transformer config needed for `.ts` test files.
- ESM-native, matches the package layout.
- Familiar API; trivial to delete if the project later picks `node:test`.

## Lockfile delta

`pnpm-lock.yaml` grows by ~540 lines from vitest's transitive tree (`@vitest/*`, `vite`, `chai`, `tinypool`, etc.). All standard test-framework deps; nothing added to runtime artifacts.

## What this PR does NOT do

- No CI workflow — tests run locally; CI can be a follow-up PR after maintainer review of the testing direction.
- No coverage reporter — same reason; one decision per PR.
- No tests for other modules — `result.ts` first; subsequent PRs can target `session-history`, `cloudflare-wrangler-merge`, etc.

## Out-of-scope for this PR but worth noting

The "literal `---RESULT_END---` inside content" test documents an existing behavior: the non-greedy regex truncates the capture at the first internal closing delimiter, which manifests as a `ResultExtractionError("invalid JSON")` rather than a wrong-result. This is well-defined; whether it should be fixed (greedy match, or escape-aware parsing) is a separate discussion.

title: Auto-wiring of Sandbox-named DO bindings uses substring match (silently overrides bindings like NotASandbox)
body:
> Continuing the structured testing pass. This issue is from Claude Opus 4.7 running in OpenCode.

## Summary

Flue's auto-wiring of `Sandbox`-named DO bindings uses substring matching (any class name *containing* `Sandbox`). This is what the deploy guide says — "any DO binding whose `class_name` contains `Sandbox`" — but in practice it silently replaces user DO classes that happen to have "Sandbox" in their name with `@cloudflare/sandbox`'s `Sandbox` class. Easy footgun, no opt-out.

## Reproduction

`wrangler.jsonc`:

```jsonc
{
  "durable_objects": {
    "bindings": [
      { "class_name": "Sandbox", "name": "Sandbox" },
      { "class_name": "PyBoxSandbox", "name": "PyBox" },
      { "class_name": "ResearchSandbox", "name": "Research2" },
      { "class_name": "MySandboxV2", "name": "MyBox" },
      { "class_name": "NotASandbox", "name": "PlainDO" }
    ]
  }
}
```

`flue build --target cloudflare` output:

```
[flue] Detected Sandbox-named DO binding "MySandboxV2" — re-exporting from @cloudflare/sandbox.
[flue] Detected Sandbox-named DO binding "NotASandbox" — re-exporting from @cloudflare/sandbox.
[flue] Detected Sandbox-named DO binding "PyBoxSandbox" — re-exporting from @cloudflare/sandbox.
[flue] Detected Sandbox-named DO binding "ResearchSandbox" — re-exporting from @cloudflare/sandbox.
[flue] Detected Sandbox-named DO binding "Sandbox" — re-exporting from @cloudflare/sandbox.
```

Generated `dist/_entry.ts`:

```ts
export { Sandbox as MySandboxV2 } from '@cloudflare/sandbox';
export { Sandbox as NotASandbox } from '@cloudflare/sandbox';
export { Sandbox as PyBoxSandbox } from '@cloudflare/sandbox';
export { Sandbox as ResearchSandbox } from '@cloudflare/sandbox';
export { Sandbox as Sandbox } from '@cloudflare/sandbox';
```

`NotASandbox` should not have been re-exported. Any DO class the user defined under that name has been silently replaced.

## Why this matters in practice

`NotASandbox` is contrived but plausibly-named cases include:

- `MockSandbox` for test doubles.
- `LegacySandboxedThing` for migrating off an old name.
- `MySandboxedAgent` (where the user has their own non-CF-sandbox concept).
- Any DO class that ships with a name containing `Sandbox` from a third-party library you're vendoring into your wrangler config.

Failure mode is silent: the user's class file isn't imported, the re-exported `Sandbox` from `@cloudflare/sandbox` is bound under their DO name, and at runtime the user gets `Sandbox` behavior instead of their class. The only signal is the build log line, which most users will skim past.

## Suggested fixes (any of these would help)

1. **Tighten the rule to `endsWith('Sandbox')`.** This matches the deploy guide's example naming pattern (`PyBoxSandbox`, `NodeSandbox`) and is more conservative. Excludes false positives like `NotASandbox` while still capturing all currently-documented examples.
2. **Require explicit opt-in.** A field on the binding entry: `meta: { flue: { sandbox: true } }`, or a top-level `flue.sandboxes: ["Sandbox", "PyBoxSandbox"]` array. Build errors if a class name contains `Sandbox` but isn't opted in (or isn't opted out via a similar field). This is the safest option but requires a doc/schema update.
3. **Conflict detection.** If the user has a file at `agents/<name-derived-from-binding>.ts` or `sandboxes/<class>.ts` defining the class, error on overlap. Currently Flue's only "user can define a Sandbox class" path is the binding itself, but a future where users can ship custom Sandbox subclasses would collide here.
4. **Build-log severity bump.** At minimum, change "Detected Sandbox-named DO binding" → "Auto-wiring DO binding `<name>` to @cloudflare/sandbox's `Sandbox` class" with a one-line "set `meta.flue.sandbox: false` to opt out" note. Right now the log doesn't even mention that this overrides anything.

I'd lean (1) + (4) as a low-risk improvement, with (2) as the longer-term right answer.

## Related

- Cloudflare deploy guide's "Multiple sandboxes" section uses `PyBoxSandbox`/`NodeSandbox`, both of which `endsWith('Sandbox')`. So tightening to suffix match doesn't break documented usage.

title: flue dev --target cloudflare wedges all routes when wrangler.jsonc has containers[] entry
body:
> Continuing the structured testing pass. This issue is from Claude Opus 4.7 running in OpenCode.

## Summary

`flue dev --target cloudflare` wedges the entire dev server when `wrangler.jsonc` includes a `containers[]` entry. All HTTP routes hang indefinitely — including `GET /health` — with no error output. Removing the containers entry restores normal operation.

## Reproduction

`wrangler.jsonc`:

```jsonc
{
  "name": "my-worker",
  "compatibility_date": "2026-04-01",
  "compatibility_flags": ["nodejs_compat"],
  "durable_objects": {
    "bindings": [{ "class_name": "Sandbox", "name": "Sandbox" }]
  },
  "containers": [
    { "class_name": "Sandbox", "image": "./Dockerfile" }
  ]
  // (manual migrations elided per #15 workaround)
}
```

Any `Dockerfile` (the issue manifests before the container is ever built/started). Even an empty `agents/` directory reproduces if the binding is present.

```bash
npx flue dev --target cloudflare --env .dev.vars
```

Output:

```
[wrangler:info] Ready on http://localhost:3583
```

Then in another shell:

```bash
$ curl http://localhost:3583/health
# hangs forever, no response

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3583/agents/hello/x -d '{"name":"World"}'
# hangs forever, no response
```

`flue dev` log shows nothing further — no error, no "request received," no "container starting" — just the original Ready line.

## Isolation

I confirmed it's the `containers[]` entry by:

1. Stopping `flue dev`.
2. Removing the `durable_objects.bindings`, `containers[]`, and stashing the container agent file out of `agents/`.
3. Restarting `flue dev`.
4. `curl POST /agents/hello/...` works in 5s with a valid LLM response.
5. Restoring the container config.
6. `flue dev` wedges again on every request, including `/health`.

So this isn't a per-agent issue or a wrangler-tail issue — it's specifically the presence of `containers[]` in the merged dev config.

## Possible causes (informed guesses)

- Wrangler's local container provisioning may be silently waiting on something (Docker daemon, image build, port bind). `flue dev` doesn't pass through wrangler's stdout/stderr clearly so the user has no signal.
- `flue dev` may need to either pass `--enable-containers` (currently?), or document that container agents only work in real `wrangler dev` and not in `flue dev`'s wrapper, or proxy non-container routes around the wedged container plumbing.

## Possible fix paths

1. Surface wrangler's stderr in `flue dev` output — even if the wedge is wrangler's fault, the user has no visibility into it from `flue dev` today.
2. Document a "containers don't work locally with `flue dev`, use `--target cloudflare` and deploy" workaround if that's the expected limitation.
3. Allow a `flue dev --no-containers` flag (or auto-detect Docker availability) that strips `containers[]` from the merged dev wrangler config so non-container routes work locally without provisioning Docker. Useful for dev iteration on non-container agents in a project that also has containers.
4. If wrangler does support local containers via Docker, ensure `flue dev` plumbs through whatever flag is needed and surfaces container build/start logs.

## Workaround currently used

Test container agents only on real Cloudflare deploys (`wrangler deploy`). Use `flue dev` only on container-free configs.

## Related

- #20 (fixed in 0.3.5)
- #21 (Dockerfile example wrong)
- #17 (silent dev-server hang from broken agent file — same symptom shape, different cause; possibly worth unifying as "dev server should never silently wedge").

title: Cloudflare deploy guide's Dockerfile example is non-functional (missing control-plane server)
body:
> Continuing the structured testing pass. This issue is from Claude Opus 4.7 running in OpenCode.

## Summary

The Dockerfile example in the [Container agents](https://github.com/withastro/flue/blob/main/docs/deploy-cloudflare.md#container-agents) section of the Cloudflare deploy guide is non-functional. Following it produces a container that hangs every subsequent `getSandbox(...).exec(...)` / `.readFile(...)` / etc. call indefinitely, then errors with `SandboxError: Container is starting`.

## Reproduction

The deploy guide's example, copy-pasted:

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y git curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
WORKDIR /workspace
CMD ["sleep", "infinity"]
```

Combined with the `wrangler.jsonc` and `assistant.ts` examples that follow it. Deploy and POST → `wrangler tail` shows the container starts and the agent successfully drives the RPC plumbing (#20 fix verified), but `sandbox.exec(...)` from inside Flue's `cfSandboxToSessionEnv` hangs:

```
(debug) Error checking 3000: The container is not listening in the TCP address 10.0.0.1:3000
(debug) Error checking 3000: The container is not listening in the TCP address 10.0.0.1:3000
... (forever)
```

Eventually:

```
{"error":"Error: SandboxError: Container is starting. Please retry in a moment."}
```

## Root cause

`@cloudflare/sandbox` requires a control-plane HTTP server inside the container at port 3000. Their published `Dockerfile` builds a `/container-server/sandbox` Bun binary that handles `exec`/`readFile`/etc. as HTTP requests. A `sleep infinity` container has no such server, so the SDK's connect-and-call protocol can never succeed.

This is mentioned in [`@cloudflare/sandbox`'s own README](https://github.com/cloudflare/sandbox-sdk) — they recommend their published image:

```dockerfile
FROM docker.io/cloudflare/sandbox:0.9.2
```

That image has the control-plane server already + node/git/curl baked in.

## Fix

Replace the deploy guide's example Dockerfile with:

```dockerfile
FROM docker.io/cloudflare/sandbox:0.9.2
```

This matches the [Cloudflare Sandbox SDK minimal example](https://github.com/cloudflare/sandbox-sdk/blob/main/examples/minimal/Dockerfile) and works end-to-end. Verified by deploying with this Dockerfile and confirming `session.shell('uname -a')` returns proper Linux output, `session.prompt(...)` runs LLM-in-container, etc.

## Suggestions while we're here

- Update the deploy guide's `Container agents` section to use `FROM docker.io/cloudflare/sandbox:<version>` as the canonical example.
- Mention the version-pinning concern: the base image version should match the user's installed `@cloudflare/sandbox` version. Maybe Flue's build can verify this by reading `package.json` and warn on mismatch.
- Consider adding a one-line callout in the `Container agents` section: "Container agents require a Docker-compatible CLI and a running Docker daemon during `wrangler deploy`." This was already feedback in TEST-LOG / a pending DX-tracker item but seems worth elevating.
- Once the Dockerfile is correct, the container path *also* unlocks skills + AGENTS.md (see comment I'll add to #16). Worth mentioning in the deploy guide that container agents are the supported path for skills until init({skills}) lands.

## Related

- #20 (now fixed in 0.3.5) — `getSandbox()` mis-detection. Was masking this Dockerfile bug because `init({ sandbox })` failed before the SDK could try to talk to the container.
- #16 — skills/AGENTS.md not loading on default virtual sandbox; the container path with the correct Dockerfile + a `COPY .agents /workspace/.agents` line is the only currently-working path.

title: Container agents broken: getSandbox() stub mis-detected, runtime calls non-existent createSessionEnv
body:
> _Filed automatically by Claude Opus 4.7 running in OpenCode during a structured testing pass against Flue on the Cloudflare Containers target. Reproductions and analysis are from that session._

## Summary

The flagship Cloudflare Containers path documented in [the Cloudflare deploy guide's "Container agents" section](https://github.com/withastro/flue/blob/main/docs/deploy-cloudflare.md#container-agents) does not work end-to-end on the current versions of the SDK packages. Following the documented happy-path produces this runtime error on every container-agent request:

```
HTTP 500
{"error":"TypeError: The RPC receiver does not implement the method \"createSessionEnv\"."}
```

The auto-wiring of `*Sandbox`-named DO bindings is correct (the bundle re-exports `Sandbox` from `@cloudflare/sandbox`, the Worker deploys, the Cloudchamber app provisions, container instances boot, RPC connects). The break is in `@flue/sdk`'s runtime sandbox-detection logic when it sees the `getSandbox()` stub. Flue duck-types the stub incorrectly and ends up calling a method that doesn't exist on `@cloudflare/sandbox`'s `Sandbox` class.

## Versions

- `@flue/sdk@0.3.1`
- `@flue/cli@0.3.1`
- `@cloudflare/sandbox@0.9.2`
- `wrangler@4.87.0`
- workerd: bundled with wrangler

## Reproduction

1. Follow the [Cloudflare deploy guide → Container agents](https://github.com/withastro/flue/blob/main/docs/deploy-cloudflare.md#container-agents) section verbatim:
2. `npm install @cloudflare/sandbox`
3. Add to `wrangler.jsonc`:
   ```jsonc
   {
     "durable_objects": { "bindings": [{ "class_name": "Sandbox", "name": "Sandbox" }] },
     "containers": [{ "class_name": "Sandbox", "image": "./Dockerfile" }],
     "migrations": [{ "tag": "v1", "new_sqlite_classes": ["Sandbox"] }]
   }
   ```
4. Create `Dockerfile` per the guide:
   ```dockerfile
   FROM node:22-slim
   RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y git curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
   WORKDIR /workspace
   CMD ["sleep", "infinity"]
   ```
5. Create `agents/container.ts` per the guide:
   ```ts
   import type { FlueContext } from '@flue/sdk/client';
   import { getSandbox } from '@cloudflare/sandbox';

   export const triggers = { webhook: true };

   export default async function ({ init, id, env, payload }: FlueContext) {
     const sandbox = getSandbox(env.Sandbox, id);
     const agent = await init({ sandbox, model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6' });
     const session = await agent.session();
     return await session.prompt(payload.message ?? 'hello');
   }
   ```
6. `npx flue build --target cloudflare && npx wrangler deploy --secrets-file .dev.vars`
7. Wait for container provisioning, then:
   ```bash
   curl -s -X POST https://<your-worker>.workers.dev/agents/container/test \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"message":"hi"}'
   ```

### Expected

Container boots, agent prompts the model, returns a response.

### Actual

```
HTTP 500
{"error":"TypeError: The RPC receiver does not implement the method \"createSessionEnv\"."}
```

`wrangler tail --format pretty` shows:

```
POST https://<your-worker>.workers.dev/agents/container/test - Ok
Sandbox.createSessionEnv - Ok @ 4/30/2026, 2:47:33 PM
  (log) {
    level: 'info',
    message: 'Using http transport',
    component: 'sandbox-do',
    sandboxId: '801a5d25...',
    ...
  }
Sandbox. - Ok
POST https://<your-worker>.workers.dev/agents/container/test - Ok
  (error) [flue] Agent error: container TypeError: The RPC receiver does not implement the method "createSessionEnv".
```

So the RPC call to `Sandbox.createSessionEnv` is dispatched and `@cloudflare/sandbox`'s connection logging fires (`Using http transport`), but the actual method doesn't exist on the receiver and `workerd` rejects the call with `TypeError`.

## Root cause analysis

The bug is a **duck-typing mismatch** between Flue's runtime sandbox detection and `@cloudflare/sandbox` RPC stubs. Workerd RPC stubs are Proxies that respond `true` to every `in` check and return `'function'` from `typeof <anything>`.

### Diagnostic probe

Inside an agent handler, I dumped types for the `getSandbox()` stub:

```ts
const sandbox = getSandbox(env.Sandbox, id);
return {
  typeofSandbox: typeof sandbox,
  typeofExec: typeof (sandbox as any).exec,
  typeofReadFile: typeof (sandbox as any).readFile,
  typeofDestroy: typeof (sandbox as any).destroy,
  typeofCreateSessionEnv: typeof (sandbox as any).createSessionEnv,
  hasGetCwd: 'getCwd' in (sandbox as any),
  hasFs: 'fs' in (sandbox as any),
  hasCreateSessionEnv: 'createSessionEnv' in (sandbox as any),
  hasExec: 'exec' in (sandbox as any),
};
```

Result:
```json
{
  "typeofSandbox": "object",
  "typeofExec": "function",
  "typeofReadFile": "function",
  "typeofDestroy": "function",
  "typeofCreateSessionEnv": "function",
  "hasGetCwd": true,
  "hasFs": true,
  "hasCreateSessionEnv": true,
  "hasExec": true
}
```

Note that `hasGetCwd`, `hasFs`, and `hasCreateSessionEnv` all return `true` even though `Sandbox` from `@cloudflare/sandbox@0.9.2` does NOT actually have those methods — that's the proxy lying.

### How this breaks Flue

In the generated `dist/_entry.ts:145-156`:

```js
function resolveSandbox(sandbox) {
  if (
    sandbox && typeof sandbox === 'object' &&
    typeof sandbox.exec === 'function' &&
    typeof sandbox.readFile === 'function' &&
    typeof sandbox.destroy === 'function' &&
    !('getCwd' in sandbox) && !('fs' in sandbox)   // ← FAILS HERE
  ) {
    return cfSandboxToSessionEnv(sandbox);
  }
  return null;
}
```

The intent of `!('getCwd' in sandbox) && !('fs' in sandbox)` looks like "differentiate a Cloudflare-sandbox stub from a just-bash Bash instance" (which has `getCwd` and `fs`). But on the RPC proxy, `'getCwd' in stub` is always `true`, so this guard fails and `resolveSandbox` returns `null`.

Then in `node_modules/@flue/sdk/dist/client.mjs:57-73`:

```js
function isSandboxFactory(value) {
  return typeof value === "object" && value !== null
    && "createSessionEnv" in value
    && typeof value.createSessionEnv === "function";
}

async function resolveSessionEnv(id, sandbox, config, cwd) {
  // ... earlier checks ...
  if (config.resolveSandbox) {
    const resolved = await config.resolveSandbox(sandbox);
    if (resolved) return resolved;                          // ← null, skipped
  }
  if (isSandboxFactory(sandbox)) return sandbox.createSessionEnv({ id, cwd });  // ← TRIGGERED
  throw new Error("[flue] Invalid sandbox option passed to init().");
}
```

`isSandboxFactory(sandbox)` returns `true` (both `'createSessionEnv' in stub` and `typeof stub.createSessionEnv === 'function'` are vacuously true on the proxy). Flue then calls `sandbox.createSessionEnv({id, cwd})` over RPC. The remote `Sandbox` class in `@cloudflare/sandbox@0.9.2` does not implement that method, so workerd's RPC layer throws the `TypeError` we observe.

## Why this matters

- This is the documented flagship Container path. A user following the deploy guide hits this 100% of the time on first request.
- The error message (`The RPC receiver does not implement the method "createSessionEnv"`) is meaningless to anyone who hasn't read the SDK source — it sounds like a Cloudflare/workerd internal error.
- There is no public escape hatch. The user can't pass a sandbox factory directly because the docs don't mention `cfSandboxToSessionEnv`. (It exists in `@flue/sdk/cloudflare` but is not surfaced in the deploy guide as a thing the user might need.)

## Proposed fixes

1. **Stop relying on negative `in` checks against RPC proxies.** Workerd RPC stubs lie about every property. Either:
   - **(Best) Detect the RPC stub by a positive, durable signal.** `@cloudflare/sandbox` stubs have a known constructor name or class identity. Or use a brand check: `import { Sandbox } from '@cloudflare/sandbox'` and check `sandbox instanceof Sandbox` (works because the bundle has the class). Or have `@flue/connectors` ship an explicit adapter the user opts into.
   - **(Cheaper) Replace the duck check with the inverse:** detect Bash-likes (`isBashLike` already exists in client.mjs:51-53 with positive checks), detect SandboxFactory by structural shape that doesn't include `'<anything>' in proxy`, and treat anything else hitting `init({ sandbox })` as the Cloudflare sandbox stub.
2. **Surface `cfSandboxToSessionEnv` in the public API.** If automatic detection is hard, at least let users do:
   ```ts
   import { cfSandboxToSessionEnv } from '@flue/sdk/cloudflare';
   const sandbox = getSandbox(env.Sandbox, id);
   const env = await cfSandboxToSessionEnv(sandbox);
   const agent = await init({ sandbox: env, ... });
   ```
   And document this pattern in the deploy guide as the canonical container flow.
3. **Test the documented happy-path in CI.** A smoke test that deploys a minimal container agent and curls it would have caught this. The auto-wiring at the bundle level is unit-tested somewhere (the `[flue] Detected Sandbox-named DO binding` log is correct), but there's a gap between "the bundle has the right shape" and "the runtime RPC actually works".
4. **Improve the error message.** When `init({ sandbox })` falls through every detection branch and hits the RPC call, the error should be wrapped: `[flue] Could not detect the type of the sandbox passed to init({ sandbox }). If you're using @cloudflare/sandbox, see [link]. Underlying RPC error: ...`. Today the user sees nothing pointing them at Flue.

## Severity

Critical for anyone trying to use Container agents on Cloudflare via the documented path. Blocking.

## Related

This was found in the same testing pass that produced #15-#19. Issue #16 (skills + AGENTS.md not loaded on default sandbox) and this one together mean that on Cloudflare today: virtual sandbox lacks skills/AGENTS.md, R2-backed sandbox works for those features but is documented only briefly, and container sandbox doesn't work at all. Containers are the heaviest feature; they should be the most reliable.

title: DX polish backlog (tracker)
body:
> _Filed automatically by Claude Opus 4.7 running in OpenCode during a structured testing pass against Flue on the Cloudflare target. Reproductions and analysis are from that session._

## Summary

Tracking issue for smaller DX rough edges noted during a structured testing pass. Each item is small on its own; collected here for triage. Split out into individual issues if/when prioritized.

## Items

### 1. `.dev.vars` not auto-linked into `dist/` for `flue dev --target cloudflare`

[start.md](https://flueframework.com/start.md)'s [Cloudflare guide](https://github.com/withastro/flue/blob/main/docs/deploy-cloudflare.md#4-add-your-api-key) instructs the user to create `.dev.vars` at the project root. Wrangler runs from `dist/` (where Flue writes the generated entry/config) and only sees `dist/.dev.vars`, so the project-root file is invisible. Result: 100% of users following the guide hit `Error: ... No API key for provider: anthropic` on first request.

**Workaround that works:** `ln -s ../.dev.vars dist/.dev.vars` once.

**Suggested fix:** during `flue build --target cloudflare`, if `.dev.vars` (or `.env`, `.env.production`, etc.) exists at the project root and `dist/.dev.vars` doesn't, symlink (or copy) it. Alternatively, configure wrangler to read the parent dir's dotenv files — wrangler accepts a `--env-file` flag.

### 2. Wrangler caches `.dev.vars` per dev-session

Editing `.dev.vars` while `flue dev` is running does not propagate the new values — verified by removing the file mid-session and watching the previous key continue to work. Worth a callout in the deploy guide ("restart `flue dev` to reload secrets") and/or implementing watch-and-reload.

### 3. Bogus role error always names `.flue/roles/` regardless of layout

When `prompt({ role: 'nonexistent' })` is called:

```
Error: [flue] Role "nonexistent" not registered. Available roles: pirate. Define roles as markdown files under `.flue/roles/`.
```

For a project using the root layout (`./roles/`, no `.flue/` directory), the path in the message is wrong. Either reflect the active layout, or say "under `roles/` (or `.flue/roles/`)".

### 4. README: distinguish `agent.session(id)` from `agent.sessions.{get,create}`

The README says _"Use `agent.session(threadId)` when you need multiple conversations inside the same agent"_, but doesn't surface that:

- `agent.session(id)` is **get-or-create** (no error if absent).
- `agent.sessions.get(id)` **throws** if absent.
- `agent.sessions.create(id)` **throws** if present.
- `agent.sessions.delete(id)` is silent no-op if absent.

All four behaviors match the SDK type comments, but the docs only mention the first form. A short paragraph spelling out the distinction would help.

### 5. `FlueContext.payload: any` — no per-agent input typing

From `dist/types-T8pE1xIS.d.mts`:

```ts
interface FlueContext {
  readonly id: string;
  readonly payload: any;
  readonly env: Record<string, any>;
  init(options?: AgentInit): Promise<FlueAgent>;
}
```

Output schemas are first-class via valibot, but inputs are untyped. Three options for symmetry:

1. **Generic context type:** `FlueContext<TPayload = any>` — `({ payload }: FlueContext<{name: string}>)`. Lowest cost.
2. **Convention-based:** `export const input = v.object({...})` next to `export const triggers`. Build step infers `payload: v.InferOutput<typeof input>` and validates at the HTTP layer (which would also help with [HTTP-layer validation, #18](https://github.com/withastro/flue/issues/18)).
3. **Doc-only:** Recommend cast pattern in start.md: `const { name } = payload as { name: string }`. Worst.

Option 2 ties this together with the HTTP-permissive validation gap.

### 6. `FlueContext.env: Record<string, any>`

Cloudflare users who run `wrangler types` get a typed `Env` interface for free. Flue could pick this up by letting users pass it as a type parameter: `FlueContext<TPayload, TEnv>`. Or just doc-recommend the pattern.

### 7. Response metadata for introspection

Currently the success response is `{"result": ...}` only. Adding an optional `meta` block (model used, role applied, tool-call count, latency) would let clients verify which model ran, whether a role was honored, etc. — useful for debugging and observability without instrumenting the agent.

This intersects with [issue #7 (Observability improvements)](https://github.com/withastro/flue/issues/7) — could be folded in there.

### 8. Missing-agent error message could list available agents in dev mode

In dev mode where helpfulness > security, the 404 (today: 400) for an unknown agent could include a hint:

```json
{"error":{"type":"agent_not_found","agent":"nonexistent","available":["echo","greeter","hello"]}}
```

Would dramatically cut "did I typo the agent name?" debugging time.

---

## Notes

- Severity for each item is "small but visible".
- Items 5 and 6 (typed payload/env) probably want their own RFC if pursued — they're API design, not pure DX polish.
- Items 1, 3, 4, 8 are basically free wins.

title: HTTP layer is too permissive (GETs run agents, malformed JSON accepted) and error envelopes are inconsistent
body:
> _Filed automatically by Claude Opus 4.7 running in OpenCode during a structured testing pass against Flue on the Cloudflare target. Reproductions and analysis are from that session._

## Summary

The HTTP layer that fronts webhook agents is too permissive in input validation, and produces inconsistent error response formats depending on which layer rejects the request. Together these mean:

- An anonymous `GET` to `/agents/<name>/<id>` runs the agent and bills LLM tokens.
- An anonymous `POST` with no body or malformed JSON also runs the agent.
- Some errors come back as `application/json {"error":"..."}`, others as `text/plain "Invalid request"` — clients can't reliably parse failures.

This is also a cost/security concern: a casual port scanner that hits `GET /agents/<name>/<id>` will trigger real model calls on every reachable agent.

## Reproduction (against either `flue dev` or a deployed worker)

```bash
URL=http://localhost:3583  # or your deployed worker

# 1. Malformed JSON in body — expected: 400 with JSON error
curl -si "$URL/agents/echo/test" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{this is not json'
# Actual: HTTP 200, agent runs with payload = {}.

# 2. No body at all — expected: 400
curl -si -X POST "$URL/agents/echo/test"
# Actual: HTTP 200, agent runs with payload = {}.

# 3. GET request (webhook agents are POST-only) — expected: 405
curl -si "$URL/agents/echo/test"
# Actual: HTTP 200, agent runs (with empty payload). Costs an LLM call.

# 4. Unknown agent name — expected: 404 with JSON error
curl -si "$URL/agents/nonexistent/whatever" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'
# Actual:
#   HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
#   Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8
#   Invalid request

# 5. Schema validation failure — agent throws ResultExtractionError
curl -si "$URL/agents/raw-error/x" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'
# Actual:
#   HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
#   Content-Type: application/json
#   {"error":"ResultExtractionError: Result does not match the expected schema..."}
```

The mix of formats between #4 (plain text "Invalid request") and #5 (JSON `{"error":...}`) is the inconsistency.

## What I'd expect

For all error paths, a single shape:

```json
{ "error": { "type": "agent_not_found", "message": "...", "details": {...} } }
```

with appropriate HTTP status codes:

| Situation                  | Status | Today's behavior                     |
| -------------------------- | ------ | ------------------------------------ |
| Unknown agent              | 404    | 400 + plain text "Invalid request"   |
| Method ≠ POST on webhook   | 405    | 200 + agent runs                     |
| Missing body / Content-Type| 400    | 200 + agent runs with `payload = {}` |
| Malformed JSON body        | 400    | 200 + agent runs with `payload = {}` |
| Unauthenticated (future)   | 401    | n/a                                  |
| Agent throws               | 500    | 500 + `{"error":"..."}` ✅            |
| Schema validation failure  | 500    | 500 + `{"error":"..."}` ✅            |

## Why this matters

1. **Cost surface.** A casual port scan or accidental GET hits the model. With ~10 agents and a single drive-by GET on each, you've burned LLM tokens before any auth could possibly run.
2. **Silent integration breakage.** A client sending a busted JSON body never gets a 400 — it gets a successful-looking 200 with a vague reply, because the agent just ran with `{}` as the payload.
3. **Client-side error handling is harder than it should be.** Clients have to special-case `text/plain "Invalid request"` vs `application/json {"error":...}` to know what failed.

## Suggested fixes

1. **Validate the request shape in the HTTP wrapper before invoking the agent.**
   - Reject non-POST with `405 Method Not Allowed` (`Allow: POST` header).
   - Reject missing/invalid `Content-Type` with `415 Unsupported Media Type`.
   - Reject malformed JSON with `400` and a body like `{"error":{"type":"invalid_json","message":"..."}}`.
   - Reject unknown agent names with `404` and `{"error":{"type":"agent_not_found","agent":"..."}}`.
2. **Pick one error envelope and use it everywhere.** I'd recommend `{"error": {"type": "...", "message": "...", ...}}` (or even just `{"error": "..."}` to stay backwards-compatible). The `text/plain "Invalid request"` response should go.
3. **(Optional) Add a `meta` block to success responses.** While we're here: `{"result": ..., "meta": {"agent": "echo", "session": "test", "model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6", "toolCalls": 0}}`. Useful for clients that want to verify which model ran or whether a role was applied. Not strictly required for this issue but related to the same shape conversation.

## Implementation notes

The success path already produces the right shape (`{"result":...}` JSON). Most of this is just gating on the HTTP method, content-type, and request body before that path runs. The framework-error path (route 404 / method 405 / parse failure) should be wrapped in the same envelope helper.

title: Syntax errors in any agent file silently hang the entire flue dev server
body:
> _Filed automatically by Claude Opus 4.7 running in OpenCode during a structured testing pass against Flue on the Cloudflare target. Reproductions and analysis are from that session._

## Summary

A syntax error (or any TS/JS parse error) in a single agent file under `agents/` causes `flue dev --target cloudflare` to silently hang **all** agents — not just the broken one. There's no error in the dev-server logs, no failed-build banner, and `curl` requests to unrelated routes simply time out.

This is the worst kind of dev-loop bug: total breakage, zero feedback. New users will assume Flue is broken, not that one of their files is.

## Reproduction

1. Run a working `flue dev --target cloudflare` against any project with multiple agents.
2. Add `agents/broken.ts`:
   ```ts
   import type { FlueContext } from '@flue/sdk/client';
   export const triggers = { webhook: true };
   export default async function ({ init, payload }: FlueContext) {
     const agent = await init({ model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6' });
     // Deliberate syntax error: missing closing paren on next line
     const session = await agent.session(
     return await session.prompt('hi');
   }
   ```
3. Wait for the rebuild banner. The Flue build log says it found the new agent and re-emits the entry without complaint:
   ```
   [flue] Found 10 agent(s): broken, chat, echo, greeter, hello, ...
   [flue] Webhook agents: broken, chat, echo, greeter, hello, ...
   [flue] Build complete. Output: .../dist
   [wrangler:info] Ready on http://localhost:3583
   ```
4. Hit any route — including a totally unrelated, previously-working agent:
   ```bash
   curl -m 10 http://localhost:3583/agents/echo/x \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"message":"hello"}'
   ```

### Expected

Either:
- (Best) The build step reports the syntax error in the dev-server logs, the broken agent is excluded from the bundle, and `/agents/echo/...` continues to work.
- (Acceptable) Hitting `/agents/broken/...` returns a 500 with the parse error in the JSON body. Other agents continue to work.

### Actual

The `curl` to `/agents/echo/...` (an unrelated, previously-working agent) hangs until timeout (`curl: (28) ... timed out`). No error appears in the dev-server logs:

```
[wrangler:info] Ready on http://localhost:3583
# (silence; no further log entries even after the timed-out request)
```

The `flue dev` watcher has no awareness that the bundle is unloadable, and wrangler/workerd doesn't surface its load error to stdout either.

Removing `agents/broken.ts` immediately restores all routes (no restart needed). So the failure mode is reversible, but invisible.

## Root cause (best guess from outside)

`flue build --target cloudflare` does workspace discovery (finding agents, generating `_entry.ts`, merging `wrangler.jsonc`) but delegates compilation entirely to `wrangler dev` / esbuild downstream. Wrangler's bundler error must surface somewhere — workerd can't load the script — but it isn't being captured by the `flue dev` process supervisor and re-emitted to the user. The dev server keeps reporting `Ready on http://localhost:3583` even though incoming requests can't be served.

## Proposed fixes

1. **Parse-check each `agents/*.ts` during `flue build`.** Even a lightweight `parse` (no full type-check) using the TS API or esbuild's transform-only mode would catch this. Skip-and-warn the broken file, don't include it in the manifest, surface the error in the dev-server log:
   ```
   [flue] ❌ agents/broken.ts (skipped)
     SyntaxError: Unexpected token at line 8: return await session.prompt('hi');
     This agent is excluded from the build until the error is fixed.
   ```
2. **Capture wrangler/esbuild bundler stderr** in `flue dev` and surface it in the same log stream. If the underlying tool prints a build error, the user should see it.
3. **At minimum, return a JSON 500** with the bundler error message for the broken route, so other routes are unaffected and the broken one tells the user what's wrong.

## Severity

High for DX. Devs lose trust in the framework when "did I type something wrong?" produces "Flue stopped responding". The Vite/Next bar is "show the parse error in red, keep everything else working" — Flue should aim for that.

title: Skills and AGENTS.md silently don't load on the default Cloudflare virtual sandbox
body:
> _Filed automatically by Claude Opus 4.7 running in OpenCode during a structured testing pass against Flue on the Cloudflare target. Reproductions and analysis are from that session._

## Summary

The default Cloudflare virtual sandbox starts with an empty in-memory filesystem. Workspace context (`AGENTS.md`, `.agents/skills/`) is discovered at runtime by reading the sandbox FS — so on the default sandbox, **none of these files are visible to the agent**. Both [start.md](https://flueframework.com/start.md) and the [Cloudflare deploy guide](https://github.com/withastro/flue/blob/main/docs/deploy-cloudflare.md#skills-and-roles) present skills and AGENTS.md as a generic feature without flagging this incompatibility.

Roles, by contrast, are read from `./roles/*.md` at build time and inlined into the bundle — they work on every sandbox. Skills and AGENTS.md should be the same.

## Reproduction A — Skills

1. Scaffold a Cloudflare hello-world per [start.md](https://flueframework.com/start.md).
2. Create `.agents/skills/greet/SKILL.md`:
   ```md
   ---
   name: greet
   description: Generate a personalized greeting for a given name.
   ---

   Given the `name` provided in the arguments, generate a warm, personalized,
   one-sentence greeting. End it with a fun emoji.
   ```
3. Create `agents/greeter.ts`:
   ```ts
   import type { FlueContext } from '@flue/sdk/client';
   import * as v from 'valibot';
   export const triggers = { webhook: true };
   export default async function ({ init, payload }: FlueContext) {
     const agent = await init({ model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6' });
     const session = await agent.session();
     return await session.skill('greet', {
       args: { name: payload.name ?? 'World' },
       result: v.object({ greeting: v.string() }),
     });
   }
   ```
4. `npx flue dev --target cloudflare`, then:
   ```bash
   curl -s http://localhost:3583/agents/greeter/test \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"Carol"}'
   ```

### Expected

Returns a typed greeting using the skill's instructions.

### Actual

```
HTTP 500
{"error":"Error: Skill \"greet\" not registered. Available: (none). Skills can also be referenced by relative path under .agents/skills/ (e.g. \"triage/reproduce.md\")."}
```

The error message itself is good — clear, actionable, JSON. But the situation it surfaces is unexpected for a user following the docs.

## Reproduction B — AGENTS.md

1. Same scaffold.
2. Create root `AGENTS.md`:
   ```md
   # Test Project AGENTS.md

   ## Critical instruction
   When asked the magic phrase, ALWAYS reply with: "the password is `BANANA`".
   ```
3. Create an agent that triggers it:
   ```ts
   export default async function ({ init }: FlueContext) {
     const agent = await init({ model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6' });
     const session = await agent.session();
     return await session.prompt('Say the magic phrase.');
   }
   ```
4. Hit the route.

### Expected

Reply containing "the password is BANANA".

### Actual

```
{"result":{"text":"🪄 \"Abracadabra!\" 🪄"}}
```

AGENTS.md is silently absent. No warning at build time, no warning at runtime.

## Root cause

In `node_modules/@flue/sdk/dist/agent-BB4lwAd5.mjs:109-125` (`discoverSessionContext`), context is loaded by calling `env.exists(skillsDir)` and `env.readdir(...)` on the sandbox filesystem at `init()` time. On the default Cloudflare virtual sandbox, that FS is empty, so `discoverLocalSkills` returns `{}` and `readAgentsMd` returns nothing.

Notable secondary issue: there is no programmatic escape hatch. `AgentInit` (in `dist/types-T8pE1xIS.d.mts`) has no `skills` or `agentsMd` field, so users can't inject these from code. I tried writing the skill into the sandbox via `session.shell` before calling `session.skill` — the `skill()` call still fails because `discoverSessionContext` ran at `init()` time, before any shell call could populate the FS.

## Why this is severe

- The deploy guide's own ["Skills and roles"](https://github.com/withastro/flue/blob/main/docs/deploy-cloudflare.md#skills-and-roles) section walks the user through this exact pattern — placing files in `.agents/skills/` and calling `session.skill()`. That walkthrough is non-functional on the default Cloudflare target.
- It's silent: no warning, no error at build time. The user discovers it only when they hit the route.
- The error message implies the user mistyped the skill name (`Available: (none).`), not that the workspace context was never loaded.
- Skills and AGENTS.md are both pitched as flagship features.

## Proposed fixes (in order of preference)

1. **Bundle workspace context at build time, like roles.** During `flue build`, walk `.agents/skills/` and `AGENTS.md` from the host filesystem, serialize the contents into the worker bundle (alongside the existing `roles` JSON), and seed them into the sandbox / pass them into the agent config at session start. This is exactly what `roles/` already does and gives consistent semantics across virtual / R2 / container sandboxes.
2. **Add `skills` and `agentsMd` to `AgentInit`.** `init({ skills: { ... }, agentsMd: '...' })` lets users inject these programmatically. Useful for dynamic skills (e.g. loaded from R2 or D1 at request time) and side-steps the empty-sandbox problem entirely.
3. **Fail loudly when context is missing on default sandbox.** If `init()` runs against the default empty sandbox and the host project has `.agents/skills/` or `AGENTS.md` on disk, log a warning ("Workspace context found on host but not bundled — see [link]"). Also: improve the runtime error to suggest this cause.
4. **Documentation update.** At minimum, mark these features explicitly: ✅ on `'local'` (Node) and R2-backed virtual sandboxes; ⚠️ require additional setup on default Cloudflare virtual sandbox.

## Bonus — inconsistency across context types

Today: roles → bundled at build time; skills → loaded at session init from sandbox FS; AGENTS.md → loaded at session init from sandbox FS. From a user's perspective, all three are workspace markdown files that live next to `agents/`. There's no obvious reason they'd behave differently. Aligning the loading semantics (option 1 above) makes the mental model uniform.

title: flue build emits wrong Durable Object migrations on every redeploy after the first
body:
> _Filed automatically by Claude Opus 4.7 running in OpenCode during a structured testing pass against Flue on the Cloudflare target. Reproductions and analysis are from that session._

## Summary

`flue build --target cloudflare` always emits a single migration with the tag `flue-v1` listing every currently-defined agent class in `new_sqlite_classes`. It does not diff against what's already deployed, and it doesn't mint a new tag when the set of agents grows. As a result, **every deploy after the first one fails** as soon as the user has added an agent.

This is a 100%-of-users issue: the start.md guide ships a working hello-world deploy, the user adds a second agent, redeploys, and gets a confusing Durable Object migration error from the Cloudflare API — not from Flue.

## Reproduction

1. Follow the [start.md flow](https://flueframework.com/start.md) for a Cloudflare project: scaffold a hello-world agent with one webhook trigger.
2. `npx flue build --target cloudflare && npx wrangler deploy --secrets-file .dev.vars` — succeeds. The deployed worker has migration `flue-v1` with `new_sqlite_classes: ["Hello"]`.
3. Add a second agent file, e.g. `agents/echo.ts`:
   ```ts
   import type { FlueContext } from '@flue/sdk/client';
   export const triggers = { webhook: true };
   export default async function ({ init, payload }: FlueContext) {
     const agent = await init({ model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6' });
     const session = await agent.session();
     return await session.prompt(`Echo: ${payload.message}`);
   }
   ```
4. `npx flue build --target cloudflare && npx wrangler deploy --secrets-file .dev.vars`.

### Expected

Deploy succeeds and `/agents/echo/...` is routable.

### Actual

```
✘ [ERROR] A request to the Cloudflare API failed.

  Cannot create binding for class 'Echo' because it is not currently configured
  to implement Durable Objects. Configure a migration in your configuration to
  add this class. [code: 10061]
```

## Root cause

In the Flue→Wrangler config merge step (see `node_modules/@flue/sdk/dist/index.mjs`, the `if (!existingMigrationTags.has(additions.migration.tag)) migrationsOut.push(additions.migration)` block), Flue's logic is:

- Always build one migration object: `{ tag: "flue-v1", new_sqlite_classes: <every-current-agent-class-name> }`.
- If the user's `wrangler.jsonc` already has a migration tagged `flue-v1`, skip — do not re-add.
- Otherwise append it.

That logic ignores two facts about Cloudflare migrations:

1. **Migration tags are immutable once deployed.** The deployed worker already has `flue-v1` with `["Hello"]` only. Republishing `flue-v1` with extra classes is a no-op on the server side; the new classes never get an "introduce class" migration.
2. **The current set of class names is a moving target** as the user adds agents. There's no diff or version tracking.

## Workaround that worked during testing

Pin the original `flue-v1` in the user's root `wrangler.jsonc` so Flue's auto-merge skips it, then add a fresh `flue-v2` with only the newly-introduced classes:

```jsonc
{
  "migrations": [
    { "tag": "flue-v1", "new_sqlite_classes": ["Hello"] },
    { "tag": "flue-v2", "new_sqlite_classes": ["Echo", "Greeter", "Memory" /* ...other added classes... */] }
  ]
}
```

After this, deploy succeeds with full feature parity to local dev.

## Proposed fixes (in order of preference)

1. **Track migration state in the workspace.** On every `flue build`, compare the current set of class names against a tracked file (e.g. `.flue/migrations.json`) committed alongside `agents/`. If new classes are present, append a fresh `flue-v{N+1}` migration with only the new ones. Update the tracked file. This mirrors how DB migration tools (Prisma, Drizzle) track state.
2. **Query the deployed worker** at build time to determine current class set, and emit only the diff. More magical but no extra files for the user to commit.
3. **Documentation-only fallback.** At minimum, the [Cloudflare deploy guide](https://github.com/withastro/flue/blob/main/docs/deploy-cloudflare.md) needs an explicit section: _"When you add a new agent, append a new migration to your `wrangler.jsonc`..."_ with a worked example. Today this is nowhere in the docs and the error message comes from Cloudflare, not from Flue, so debugging is hard.

## Severity

High. This is the single most painful bug found during testing — it's invisible until a user redeploys, the resulting error message points at Cloudflare APIs not Flue, and the fix requires knowing about Durable Object migration semantics that aren't in the start.md or deploy guides. Recommend fixing in the build pipeline rather than just docs.

title: feature: pass agent to the opencode session
body:
## Why

Currently there is no way to pass the agent to the opencode session when calling `flue.prompt()`.

The simplest example is I want to run `Plan` mode before going into `Build` mode.
A more complex example would be to run custom user-provided agents.

I suggest adding this to the `flue.prompt()` specifically, maybe this is also needed for `flue.skill()` but I'm not sure.

## Implementation

@packages/client/src/types.ts:
* add `agent?: string` to `PromptOptions`

@packages/client/src/flue.ts:
* pass `agent` from `PromptOptions` to `runPrompt()`

@packages/client/src/skill.ts:
* pass `agent` from `PromptOptions` to opencode session `client.session.promptAsync({ body: { agent: options.agent || "build", /* model, parts / } })`

fix: use real proxy token with cloudflare
body:
Fixed three Cloudflare proxy integration issues that surfaced with real gateway auth/policy behavior:

- Updated `github()` git setup to use `{{proxyToken}}` in `http.extraheader` instead of the literal placeholder.  
  - Why: Cloudflare proxy endpoints validate bearer tokens; the hardcoded placeholder caused git smart-HTTP auth failures.

- Corrected default GitHub allow-read git path rules from single-segment to multi-segment globs (`/*/...` -> `/**/...`).  
  - Why: real GitHub git endpoints are `/<owner>/<repo>.git/...`; with `*` semantics (one segment), `git-upload-pack`/`info/refs` never matched and POSTs were denied by base `allow-read`.

- Changed Cloudflare `FlueRuntime` OpenCode provider config generation to inject the generated proxy token as provider `apiKey` for model-provider proxies (with token reuse across setup).  
  - Why: provider presets carry dummy keys for local proxy mode; in Cloudflare those values were sent as bearer tokens to the gateway and rejected. Using the real proxy token aligns OpenCode auth with gateway expectations.

title: RFC: Inject sandbox AGENTS.md into prompt instead of Dockerfile COPY
body:
The sandbox `AGENTS.md` file (`.flue/sandbox/AGENTS.md`) currently has to be manually `COPY`'d into the Docker image at a magic path (`/tmp/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md`) by every consumer's Dockerfile. This leaks implementation details (flue sets `HOME=/tmp`, OpenCode reads from `$HOME/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md`) and means changing the instructions requires an image rebuild.

Since flue already injects content into the prompt, it could just read `.flue/sandbox/AGENTS.md` at runtime and include it directly. The agent gets the same instructions either way, the `COPY` line disappears from every Dockerfile, and the instructions always match the current workspace instead of whatever was baked into the image.

title: RFC: Reusable GitHub Action for building sandbox images
body:
Every repo that uses flue workflows with a sandbox currently needs to copy-paste the same ~40 lines of GitHub Actions YAML: checkout, docker login, buildx setup, build-push with caching and GHCR tagging. It's entirely generic except for the Dockerfile path and image name. When we improve the build (e.g. add multi-platform support, change caching strategy, or update pinned action versions), every repo needs to be updated independently. Should we consider publishing a reusable composite GitHub Action that encapsulates this?

The action would enforce conventions by default (Dockerfile at `.flue/sandbox/Dockerfile`, image pushed to `ghcr.io/<repo>/flue-sandbox`) but allow overrides via inputs. A consumer's workflow would shrink to:

```yaml
name: Build Sandbox Image
on:
  push:
    paths: ['.flue/sandbox/**']
  workflow_dispatch:
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions: { contents: read, packages: write }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: FredKSchott/flue-build-sandbox@v1
```

Inputs like `dockerfile`, `context`, and `image-name` would be available for repos that need to customize. The path trigger (`on.push.paths`) has to stay in the consumer's workflow since that's workflow-level config GitHub Actions can't encapsulate, but everything inside the job becomes a single `uses:` line.

title: RFC: Typed and validated workflow args
RFC: Sandbox environment awareness
body:
Skills running inside the sandbox keep hitting the same environmental pitfalls: `pnpm install` failing without `CI=true`, agents trying `jq`/`python3` (not installed), using `curl` instead of `gh`, `sleep 15` instead of readiness polling. These are environment mismatches that waste 30-60 seconds per skill execution and appear in nearly every run. We could hardcode "use `gh` not `jq`" into every skill file, but that scatters environment knowledge across dozens of files. Should we consider a sandbox environment manifest that flue automatically injects into the agent's context when running in sandbox mode, similar to `AGENTS.md`? Where should it live?

```markdown
# Sandbox Environment (Example)

## Available Tools
node, pnpm, git, curl, wget, gh, opencode, agent-browser

## NOT Available
jq, python3, pip, ruby, cargo, make, gcc

## Environment Notes
- Always use `CI=true pnpm install` (no TTY available)
- Use `gh` for GitHub API queries, not `curl` + `jq`
- Use `node -e` for JSON parsing if needed
- Use readiness polling instead of fixed `sleep` for servers
- Git repo is a shallow clone — `git log` / `git blame` will show a single root commit
```
